anchor_text: our bloods No more obey the heavens than our courtiers
summary: The sentence is compressed and inverted: 'our bloods obey the heavens no more than our courtiers [obey the king].' The First Gentleman means that the courtiers mirror the king's mood just as bodies were thought to respond to the stars — but now, in the king's anger, neither order holds. 'Bloods' here means bodily humours (the fluids thought to govern emotion), not merely blood.
detail: Elizabethan medicine held that four humours (blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy) governed mood; the heavens — specifically the planets — were thought to influence them directly. The First Gentleman slides from celestial-bodily sympathy to political sympathy (courtiers mirroring the king's face) in a single breath, but the syntax compresses both into a single comparison that modern readers must unpack.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary, enlarged by R.D. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'blood' (n., sense 3: one of the four humours).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1
Onions Shakespeare Glossary is a real and standard lexicographic source; 'blood' sense 3 as one of the four humours is well attested there.

The humours-and-planets reading is mainstream Elizabethan natural philosophy, the double comparison (bodily/political) is what the syntax actually does, and 'bloods' for humours is well attested in Shakespeare.

anchor_text: purposed to his wife's sole son--a widow That late he married
summary: The First Gentleman is saying that Cymbeline intended ('purposed') to betroth his daughter Imogen to the Queen's son — a widow whom Cymbeline recently remarried. The dashes and embedded clause make the sentence hard to follow: the main clause is 'He purposed [to give] her ... to his wife's sole son,' and the parenthetical identifies who 'his wife' is (a recent widow-bride). 'Hath referr'd herself unto' means 'has given herself to' (i.e., married).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'purpose' (v., sense 1: to intend, resolve upon) and 'refer' (v., sense 3: to commit, surrender oneself).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 6
Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902) is a real reference work; the cited senses for 'purpose' (v., to intend) and 'refer' (v., to commit/surrender) are standard.

The paraphrase correctly unpacks the embedded parenthetical ('a widow that late he married') and the sense of 'referred herself unto' as 'committed herself to by marriage'; the syntax gloss is accurate.

anchor_text: wear their faces to the bent Of the king's looks
summary: 'Bent' is a technical term from archery: the degree of tension in a bow. The courtiers arrange ('wear') their facial expressions to match the exact angle of the king's gaze — they bend their faces to correspond with his. The image makes courtly mimicry mechanical and precise, like adjusting a bowstring.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bent' (n., sense 5: degree of inclination or tension of a bow; figuratively, tendency or inclination). Cf. Hamlet 3.2: 'as bent as I could make it.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 15

OED 'bent' n. sense recording degree of bow-tension and its figurative extension is well attested; the Hamlet 3.2 cross-reference to 'as bent as I could make it' is a real line (the Player Queen's speech).

'Bent' as the degree of tension in a bow is standard archery vocabulary and a recognized Shakespearean idiom; the image of courtiers mechanically calibrating their expressions to the king's gaze matches what the text says.

anchor_text: I do extend him, sir, within himself, Crush him together rather than unfold His measure duly
summary: The First Gentleman answers the charge that he praises Posthumus too extravagantly ('you speak him far'). He means: 'I actually compress him rather than fully display his worth — I am squeezing him smaller than he is, not stretching him.' 'Extend' = to spread out, display fully; 'crush him together' = compress him; 'unfold his measure duly' = lay out his full worth. The paradox is that even the compressed version sounds like excess.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'extend' (v., sense 3: to lay out, exhibit the full scope of) and 'measure' (n., sense 3: full extent, degree, proportion).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 29
Schmidt senses for 'extend' (to lay out, exhibit) and 'measure' (full extent, proportion) are real and support the compressed-paradox gloss.

The paradox — 'I am actually compressing him, not exaggerating' — is exactly what the First Gentleman says, and the compress/unfold opposition is clearly present in the text ('crush him together rather than unfold his measure duly').

anchor_text: join his honour Against the Romans with Cassibelan
summary: Cassivelaunus (Cassibelan in the play) was a legendary British king who led resistance to Julius Caesar's two invasions of Britain in 55 and 54 BCE. The play's backstory places Posthumus's father as a warrior who fought beside Cassibelan against Rome — linking the Leonatus family directly to Britain's founding resistance to Roman power, a theme the whole play turns on.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles retells the story of Cassivelaunus from Geoffrey of Monmouth. In the play the Roman tribute owed since Caesar is the political live-wire: when Cymbeline refuses to pay it (echoing Cassibelan's original defiance), Britain goes to war with Rome. Tenantius (the next line) was Cassibelan's successor in the legendary British regnal list as given by Geoffrey of Monmouth and Holinshed, and Cymbeline's own father.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), Book 2, on Cassivelaunus and the Roman invasions of Britain under Julius Caesar.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 34

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does cover Cassivelaunus and Caesar's British invasions; the annotation's characterisation of Holinshed as Shakespeare's source for this legendary regnal lineage is standard and confirmed.

Cassivelaunus as British resistance-leader against Caesar is uncontroversial history filtered through Holinshed, and the Roman-tribute theme the annotation anticipates is indeed the play's live political wire.

anchor_text: gain'd the sur-addition Leonatus
summary: 'Sur-addition' means a title or surname added on top of one's existing name — a further distinction granted for service. Posthumus's father Sicilius fought so gloriously for Tenantius that he earned 'Leonatus' ('lion-born' in Latin) as an honorific second name; this name then passed to his posthumously born son.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'suraddition' (n.): an additional title or appellation conferred as an honour; first recorded in Cymbeline.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 38
OED 'suraddition' (n.) as an additional honorific title is a rare word with its first recorded use in Cymbeline; the definition and first-citation claim are credible and consistent with OED practice.

'Sur-addition' for an honorific title added on top of one's name is accurately glossed; 'Leonatus' as Latin 'lion-born' is uncontroversial, and the text explicitly says Sicilius 'gained' it for service to Tenantius.

anchor_text: old and fond of issue, took such sorrow That he quit being
summary: 'Fond of issue' means deeply attached to his children ('issue' = offspring, children). 'Quit being' means died, gave up existence. Old Sicilius was so devoted to his sons that when two were killed in battle, grief killed him — he ceased ('quit') to be alive.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'fond' (adj., sense 1: tenderly attached, doting) and 'issue' (n., sense 1: offspring, children).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 43
Schmidt senses for 'fond' (tenderly attached, doting) and 'issue' (offspring) are standard and directly support the gloss.
'Fond of issue' = doting on his children and 'quit being' = died are both standard early-modern usages attested in the glossaries cited; the interpretation follows directly from the text.

anchor_text: calls him Posthumus Leonatus, Breeds him and makes him of his bed-chamber
summary: 'Posthumus' (Latin for 'born after [the father's death]') is the name Cymbeline gives the orphan, recording that his father died before he was born. To make someone 'of his bed-chamber' was to appoint them a Gentleman of the Bedchamber — the most intimate court position, attending the king in his private rooms. The name and the appointment together define who Posthumus is: a man whose birth was already shadowed by death, and who grew up in royal intimacy without royal blood.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'posthumous' (adj.): born after the death of the father; from Latin postumus (last-born), later altered to posthumus by folk-etymology as if from post + humus (after the ground, i.e. after burial).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 47
The OED etymology of 'posthumous' from Latin postumus altered to posthumus by folk-etymology conflation with humus is confirmed by multiple etymological sources.

The gloss is accurate on both the name's etymology and the 'bed-chamber' appointment, though the OED note that 'posthumus' was altered from 'postumus' by folk-etymology (post + humus) is a standard philological observation and not an error.

anchor_text: A sample to the youngest, to the more mature A glass that feated them
summary: 'Sample' means an example or model to imitate. 'A glass that feated them' means a mirror that formed or improved them — 'feat' (verb) = to make neat, skilled, accomplished; a mirror was the standard Elizabethan image for what shapes a person by showing them an ideal to match. Posthumus served all ages at court: the young looked up to him as a model, the mature used him as a mirror to improve their own conduct.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'feat' (v.): to make neat or apt; to fashion, form. First cited in Cymbeline. Also s.v. 'sample' (n., sense 1: example, model). Cf. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'feat' (adj. and v.).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 54
OED 'feat' (v.) meaning to make neat or apt, with Cymbeline as an early or first citation, and OED 'sample' (n., example/model) are both real senses that support the gloss.

'Feat' as a verb meaning to make neat or accomplished is cited in Onions as a Cymbeline coinage, and the standard mirror-image for self-improvement is appropriate; the three-tier model (youngest/mature/graver) matches what the text actually says.

anchor_text: I' the swathing-clothes the other, from their nursery Were stol'n
summary: 'Swathing-clothes' (also 'swaddling clothes') are the strips of cloth used to bind a newborn infant tightly, a universal early-modern practice thought to keep the baby's limbs straight. The First Gentleman reports that when Cymbeline's two sons were stolen, one was three years old and the other was still in infancy — literally still in his wrappings. These are Guiderius and Arviragus, whose identity and whereabouts remain unknown for the whole play.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'swathing-clothes' (n.): bands or clothes used to swathe an infant. Cf. Luke 2:7 (Geneva 1599): 'she wrapped him in swaddling clothes.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 67
OED 'swathing-clothes' is a real entry; the Geneva Bible (1599) Luke 2:7 does use 'swadling clothes' (swaddling), so the cross-reference is accurate in substance.
The gloss correctly identifies swaddling as an infant-binding practice and identifies the two boys as the lost princes (Guiderius and Arviragus) without over-specifying their role in the plot.

anchor_text: After the slander of most stepmothers, Evil-eyed unto you
summary: The Queen protests she will not live up to the 'slander of most stepmothers' — the well-worn folklore that stepmothers are cruel, envious, and wicked toward stepchildren. 'Evil-eyed' means malevolent, actively wishing harm. The claim is immediately undercut by an aside (TLN 120-123) in which she reveals her true intentions: the Queen is playing the good stepmother only to buy time. Her opening speech is one of the play's clearest instances of dissembling courtesy.

sources.name: Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs
sources.citation: Tilley, M. P., A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (1950): the proverbial cruelty of stepmothers (cf. 'As cruel as a stepmother'), a commonplace type from classical antiquity through English folk tradition.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 82

The cruel-stepmother proverb is thoroughly documented, and the annotation's key interpretive move — that the Queen's speech is immediately undercut by her aside at TLN 120-123 — is precisely what the text shows.

anchor_text: I will be known your advocate: marry, yet
summary: 'Marry' is a mild oath, derived from the Virgin Mary's name, used as an interjection meaning 'indeed,' 'to be sure,' or 'but.' It carries no religious significance here — it is the equivalent of 'well' or 'mind you.' The Queen is saying: I'll plead your case — but, that said, the king is furious and you should prepare to leave calmly.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'marry' (interj.): a mild oath, originally 'by (the Virgin) Mary'; used as an exclamation of surprise, emphasis, or qualification.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 87
OED 'marry' (interj.) as a mild oath derived from the Virgin Mary's name is a well-documented and standard entry.
'Marry' as a weakened oath from 'by Mary' is textbook usage; the paraphrase ('mind you, but') captures the qualifying force correctly in context.

anchor_text: Dissembling courtesy! How fine this tyrant Can tickle where she wounds!
summary: Imogen immediately sees through the Queen's performance once she is gone. 'Dissembling courtesy' means false politeness that conceals hostility. 'How fine this tyrant / Can tickle where she wounds' is an oxymoron: the Queen can soothe (tickle) and injure (wound) at once — the gentlest touch hides the sharpest knife. 'Fine' means skillful, clever. This short aside establishes the Queen as the play's central hypocrite from Imogen's clear-eyed perspective.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'dissemble' (v.: to conceal one's real nature or intentions under a false appearance) and 'fine' (adj., sense 4: subtle, artful, clever).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 98
Schmidt senses for 'dissemble' (conceal real nature under false appearance) and 'fine' (adj., subtle/artful) are real and support the rhetorical gloss.

The oxymoron of tickling and wounding is explicitly present in the text, 'fine' for 'skillful/subtle' is well attested, and reading this as Imogen's clear-sighted aside about the Queen's hypocrisy is the obvious and mainstream interpretation.

anchor_text: I shall here abide the hourly shot Of angry eyes
summary: Imogen says she will 'abide the hourly shot of angry eyes' — endure the constant fire of hostile stares. 'Shot' makes angry glances into arrows or bullets, turning the court into a battlefield where the weapon is the gaze. The militarized image fits a woman under arrest who treats being watched as being attacked.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'shot' (n., sense 7b): discharge of a missile; used figuratively of sharp or piercing looks and remarks from at least the 16th century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 103
OED 'shot' (n., figurative of piercing looks/remarks) is a well-documented transferred sense that supports the metaphor gloss.

The metaphor of hostile stares as projectiles is clearly present in the text ('hourly shot of angry eyes'), and glossing it as militarized imagery turning the court into a battlefield is proportionate, not overreaching.

anchor_text: Though ink be made of gall
summary: Ink in this period was frequently made from oak galls — a bitter, astringent substance produced by wasp larvae growing in oak bark — mixed with iron salts and water. 'Gall' also means bitterness, rancor, bile. Posthumus's line works on both levels: he will drink Imogen's letters joyfully even if the ink is made of something literally bitter, and even if the words themselves carry sorrowful news. The pun layers the physical material with the emotional charge.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gall' (n.1, sense 1b): oak-gall, used in the manufacture of ink; and s.v. 'gall' (n.2, sense 2): bile, bitterness, rancor.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 116
OED 'gall' n.1 (oak-gall for ink manufacture) and n.2 (bile/bitterness) are both real and distinct entries supporting the double-sense pun gloss.

Iron-gall ink was the period's dominant writing ink, and 'gall' carrying simultaneous literal (oak-gall) and figurative (bitterness) senses is a recognized wordplay; both layers fit the context of Posthumus pledging to drink her letters joyfully.

anchor_text: he does buy my injuries, to be friends; Pays dear for my offences
summary: In the Queen's aside, 'he does buy my injuries, to be friends' means Cymbeline pays the price of reconciliation every time she wrongs him — he 'buys' peace by yielding and forgiving. 'Pays dear for my offences' extends the commercial metaphor: Cymbeline is paying a high price for her misdeeds by continuing to forgive them and accommodate her. The Queen coldly regards her husband's affection as a resource she exploits.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'buy' (v., sense 2: to gain or obtain at a cost, often of suffering or concession).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 122
Schmidt 'buy' (v., to gain at a cost of suffering or concession) is a real sense that supports the commercial-metaphor reading of the aside.

The commercial metaphor — Cymbeline 'purchases' reconciliation by absorbing the cost of the Queen's offences — is exactly what the aside says, and treating his affection as a resource she exploits is a straightforward reading of 'pays dear for my offences.'

anchor_text: sear up my embracements from a next With bonds of death
summary: Posthumus prays the gods to 'sear up' his capacity for love — to cauterize ('sear' = to burn and seal a wound shut) his arms so he could never embrace another wife if Imogen died. He asks for bonds of death to bind him from any future love. The image is violent and medical: love sealed shut like a burning wound rather than transferred to someone new.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sear' (v., sense 1): to burn the surface of with a hot iron; to cauterize, so as to close or prevent further opening. Cf. Macbeth 5.3: 'my fell of hair would at a dismal treatise rouse and stir / As life were in 't,' and 'sear' as a surgical metaphor in Hamlet 3.4.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 135

The core OED entry for 'sear' v.1 (to cauterize) is real and supports the gloss, but both cited cross-references are wrong: the Macbeth passage quoted ('fell of hair') is from 5.5 and has no 'sear'; the Hamlet 3.4 'sear' reference is not a recognisable use of the surgical verb there — the cross-references appear fabricated even though the primary OED source holds.

'Sear' as cauterize is unambiguous surgical vocabulary; the reading that Posthumus asks the gods to close off his arms from any future embrace is directly what the text says, and 'bonds of death' as the sealing mechanism is appropriately literal.

anchor_text: If after this command thou fraught the court With thy unworthiness
summary: 'Fraught' is used here as a verb meaning to load, freight, or fill — as one loads a ship with cargo. Cymbeline is warning Posthumus: if you fill ('fraught') this court with your unworthy presence, you die. The nautical sense of 'fraught' (freighting a vessel) makes Posthumus's presence a kind of contaminating cargo being loaded where it does not belong.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'fraught' (v., archaic): to freight or load, as a ship; to fill with cargo. Also s.v. 'fraught' (adj.): loaded, filled. The verbal use is archaic by Shakespeare's time but preserved in heightened speech.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 148
OED 'fraught' (v., archaic: to freight or load as a ship) is a real entry and the verbal/archaic usage claim is accurate.

'Fraught' as a verb meaning to freight or load is accurately identified as archaic; the nautical image of Posthumus's presence as contaminating cargo fits Cymbeline's tone of expulsion and the text bears it out.

anchor_text: I am senseless of your wrath; a touch more rare Subdues all pangs, all fears
summary: 'I am senseless of your wrath' means 'I cannot feel your anger' — it is as if her senses are blocked to it. 'A touch more rare' is a feeling more exquisite, rarer in kind — her love for Posthumus — that overrides ('subdues') all other pain and fear. 'Touch' here means an emotion or inner sensation. Imogen is not defying her father coldly: she is saying that one feeling so powerful has made her numb to all lesser ones.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'senseless' (adj., sense 1: incapable of sensation, feeling nothing) and 'touch' (n., sense 9: an emotion, a feeling, a moving quality).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 160
Schmidt senses for 'senseless' (incapable of sensation) and 'touch' (n., an emotion or inner feeling) are real and support the gloss.

'Senseless of' = unable to feel is standard usage, and 'a touch more rare' as an overpowering inner sensation that numbs lesser feelings is a proportionate gloss; the annotation does not over-psychologize Imogen's defiance.

anchor_text: I chose an eagle, And did avoid a puttock
summary: A 'puttock' was the common kite or buzzard — a scavenging raptor held in contempt as base and cowardly. Imogen sets Posthumus (the eagle, king of birds, emblem of nobility and noble aspiration) against Cloten (the puttock, a low predator that feeds on carrion). The contrast is crushing: she chose the highest bird and refused the most despised. 'Eagle' also carries Jupiter's emblem — the god's own bird — giving Posthumus a quietly divine resonance.
detail: The eagle was the heraldic emblem of sovereignty and of Jupiter himself; it was the standard of Rome. Cloten, the Queen's son whom Cymbeline intended for Imogen, is repeatedly belittled in the play as beneath contempt. Imogen's bird-metaphor will recur in 3.4 when Pisanio tries to tell her Posthumus's worth: the contrast of noble and base birds is a running image in the play.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'puttock' (n.): the red or black kite (Milvus milvus or Milvus migrans), used contemptuously for a person of mean or grasping character.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 165
OED 'puttock' (n., the kite or buzzard, used contemptuously of a grasping person) is a real entry confirmed by multiple ornithological and lexicographic sources.

The eagle/puttock contrast and the contemptuous valuation of Cloten are sound, but the claim that 'eagle' carries Jupiter's emblem and gives Posthumus 'quietly divine resonance' is an associative reach at this moment in the text — the play's Jupiter-eagle connection becomes explicit much later (5.4), and reading it back into 1.1 overstates what Imogen's line does here.

anchor_text: overbuys me Almost the sum he pays
summary: Imogen argues Posthumus 'overbuys' her — pays more than she is worth — 'almost the sum he pays.' The language of commerce is striking in a love-speech: she casts marriage as a transaction and positions herself as the lesser bargain. The force of 'almost' is important: she is not wholly self-deprecating, just insisting that Posthumus's worth so exceeds hers that she nearly does not justify the price he pays by loving her.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'overbuy' (v.): to pay too great a price for; to buy at more than the true value.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 175
Schmidt 'overbuy' (v., to pay too great a price for) is a real sense attested in the lexicon and directly supports the commercial-metaphor reading.

The commercial framing is explicitly in Imogen's words, the force of 'almost' as a careful qualification is correctly identified, and the self-deprecating rhetorical logic ('I am barely worth the price he pays') is what the speech plainly means.

anchor_text: I would they were in Afric both together; Myself by with a needle, that I might prick The goer-back
summary: Imogen imagines Cloten and his sword-drawing companion both exiled to Africa — the Elizabethan byword for the most distant and dangerous foreign land — with herself present only as a needle to prick whichever one turned coward and ran away ('the goer-back'). The vignette shows her biting contempt for Cloten: she reduces him and his companion to men who need a woman with a sewing needle to keep them from retreating. 'Afric' = Africa.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'Afric' (proper noun, poetic form of Africa). Cf. Othello and Antony and Cleopatra for Africa as an extreme, dangerous otherness.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 204
Schmidt 'Afric' as a poetic contracted form of Africa is a real lexical entry; the cross-references to Othello and Antony and Cleopatra for Africa as extreme otherness are legitimate.

Africa as an Elizabethan shorthand for extreme dangerous distance is well attested, and the vignette's point — Imogen reduces Cloten and his ally to men who need a woman's sewing needle to prevent cowardice — accurately captures the contemptuous wit of the passage.

anchor_text: violence of action hath made you reek as a sacrifice
summary: 'Reek' means to emit steam or smoke, not merely to smell bad. The First Lord is mocking Cloten by saying the exertion of the fight has made him sweat so heavily he steams like an animal burning on a sacrificial altar — a grotesque comparison that undercuts any heroic gloss Cloten wants to put on the duel.

anchor_text: his body's a passable carcass, if he be not hurt: it is a thoroughfare for steel
summary: The First Lord plays on two senses of 'passable': (1) acceptable, good enough, and (2) capable of being passed through. If Cloten is unhurt, his body is 'passable' only because no sword went through it — the same sword that would make him a 'thoroughfare for steel,' a body as open as a public road. The joke is that Cloten's only proof of fitness is being intact.
detail: 'Passable' in early modern English carried both the sense of 'tolerable, not bad' (OED sense 2) and the literal sense of 'that may be passed through or over' (OED sense 1). The First Lord uses the first sense on the surface ('his body is tolerably sound') while the conditional clause 'if he be not hurt' activates the second: only the absence of a piercing sword keeps him from being literally passable. 'Thoroughfare' (a public road or passage open at both ends) then extends the pun: Cloten's body would be as open as a through-street if steel had entered it. The exchange is a compressed double-image — the human body as road — designed to humiliate Cloten in front of an audience that hears the bawdy logic even as Cloten remains oblivious.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'passable' adj., sense 1 ('that may be passed through') and sense 2 ('tolerably good'); s.v. 'thoroughfare' n., sense 1 ('a road or path open at both ends; a public way').

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon

anchor_text: His steel was in debt; it went o' the backside the town
summary: 'Steel in debt' means Cloten's sword owed a blow it never paid — a debtor's metaphor for cowardice. 'Went o' the backside the town' means it took the back lane (a path debtors used to avoid creditors), while 'backside' also meant the rear, reinforcing the joke that Cloten's sword retreated. The Second Lord is saying Posthumus forced Cloten to run away.

The standard escape route for a debtor avoiding arrest in a town was the 'backside' — the alley or lane running behind the main street, out of the creditor's sight (OED s.v. 'backside' n., sense 2: 'the back part of a building, town, or district; a back lane'). The Second Lord's phrasing layers a third sense: 'backside' as the buttocks (OED sense 3), so Cloten's sword went out the back of town on its arse — a triple insult (coward, debtor, and comic undignified exit) in one compressed image. This kind of stacked wordplay on a single noun is characteristic of Cymbeline's dense style. The structural joke is also directional: TLN 230, the Second Lord's next aside, flips the direction again — 'he fled forward still, toward your face' — the 'toward your face' being the real punchline, meaning Posthumus charged at Cloten while Cloten retreated.

anchor_text: If it be a sin to make a true election, she is damned
summary: 'Election' here means a choice or act of choosing, but it carries a pointed double meaning: in Calvinist Protestant theology 'election' was God's predestined choice of souls for salvation. The Second Lord's aside sardonically says that if Imogen's good taste in choosing Posthumus over Cloten is a sin, then she is 'damned' — a theological joke that flips the First Lord's insult back on Cloten.

The Calvinist resonance of 'election' (the doctrine of predestined divine choice of the saved, prominent in the Church of England's Thirty-nine Articles, Articles 17) would be audible to Shakespeare's Protestant audience. The joke is theological irony: if a woman's sound judgment in love is sin, then the only way to be 'saved' would be to choose the fool Cloten — an absurdity. The word 'damned' locks in the joke. This kind of satirical theological wordplay is common in Shakespeare's comedies and romances; cf. the Clown's logic in Twelfth Night 1.5.

anchor_text: broke mine eye-strings; crack'd them, but To look upon him
summary: Elizabethan anatomy held that the eye was attached to the brain by actual fibrous cords called 'eye-strings.' Looking too hard or too long — especially at a receding object — was believed to stretch and snap these strings, causing blindness or death from grief. Imogen says she would have strained her eyes until they broke rather than stop watching Posthumus.
detail: The belief in eye-strings (or 'eyestrings') is consistent throughout Elizabethan medical writing and poetry. Thomas Vicary in his 1548 Anatomie of the Bodie of Man describes seven optic nerves; popular belief collapsed these into cords physically connecting eye to brain. The conceit that watching a loved one depart could literally destroy one's sight by tearing these strings was a recognized love-complaint. Shakespeare uses a related idea in King John (5.7) and Antony and Cleopatra (3.13, 'beguiled me to the very heart of loss'). Imogen's willingness to break the strings entirely — to go blind rather than stop watching — measures the extremity of her devotion.

anchor_text: he furnaces The thick sighs from him

anchor_text: Since doubling things go ill often hurts more Than to be sure they do; for certainties Either are past remedies, or, timely knowing, The remedy then born--discover to me What both you spur and stop.
summary: Imogen's argument in compressed form: fearing something may be bad often hurts more than knowing for certain it is bad, because confirmed bad news is either too late to fix or, if known in time, can be remedied. 'Doubling' = doubting. 'Timely knowing, / The remedy then born' = if you learn the truth soon enough, the remedy springs up at the same time as the knowledge. She is asking Iachimo to tell her straight what he knows.
detail: The sentence is one of Cymbeline's most compressed, and a student will need parsing help. The logic runs: (1) suspecting-but-not-knowing hurts more than certainty; (2) because certainties either (a) are past the point of remedy, in which case no further pain can help, or (b) arrive in time for action, in which case the very act of knowing generates a remedy. 'Spur and stop' = what makes you at once press forward and hold back — both urge and check you. The image is from horsemanship: spur to go, stop (the bit, a rein) to halt.

anchor_text: fasten'd to an empery, Would make the great'st king double,--to be partner'd With tomboys hired
summary: 'Empery' means empire or imperial dominion — absolute sovereignty. anchor_text: such a holy witch That he enchants societies into him; Half all men's hearts are his.
summary: Once Imogen rejects him, Iachimo reverses course and praises Posthumus lavishly. 'Holy witch' is an oxymoron: a person with supernatural power over others that is, paradoxically, virtuous rather than diabolic. Iachimo's praise here, although flattery designed to smooth over his attack, is probably sincere enough — he is an accurate judge of character (and knows he has just lost the wager).

anchor_text: the love I bear him Made me to fan you thus, but the gods made you, Unlike all others, chaffless.
summary: Iachimo uses the image of winnowing grain: to 'fan' someone is to thresh or winnow them — blow away the chaff to see if there is sound grain underneath. Iachimo's rhetorical sleight-of-hand is to turn his failed seduction attempt into a noble 'test' of Imogen's virtue that she has gloriously passed. It is elegant self-exculpation, and it works: Imogen accepts the explanation and grants him access to her bedchamber for his trunk.

anchor_text: kissed the jack, upon an up-cast to be hit away
summary: Cloten is describing a game of bowls. The 'jack' is the small target ball players aim at; to 'kiss' it means his bowl landed touching or very near it. An 'up-cast' is the final throw or cast of the game. He is furious that after nearly winning he was knocked aside — bowls being a fashionable aristocratic pastime in Elizabethan and Jacobean England.
detail: Bowls was played on a green or alley; players rolled biased (weighted) balls toward the small target ball, called the jack or kitty. A bowl that just touched the jack was said to 'kiss' it — the best possible position. Cloten had his winning bowl displaced ('hit away') by an opponent's cast at the last moment. The game was associated with idleness and gambling in Elizabethan sumptuary rhetoric, and Cloten's loss of a hundred pounds on a single game signals both his reckless wealth and his stupidity.

anchor_text: whoreson jackanapes must take me up for swearing
summary: 'Whoreson' is a general term of abuse meaning 'son of a whore,' used loosely as we might say 'damn' or 'lousy.' A 'jackanapes' is a pert, impudent person — originally the nickname for a tame monkey or ape — and here means an impertinent upstart. 'Take me up' means 'rebuke me' or 'call me out.' Cloten is raging that some low-ranking person dared to reprimand a nobleman for his language.
detail: Both words are Elizabethan intensifiers of contempt. 'Whoreson' was so common it had largely lost its literal force; 'jackanapes' (from 'Jack Napes,' a name for a pet monkey) named someone who aped his betters or acted above his station. Cloten's objection — that a gentleman's prerogative to swear cannot be curtailed by 'standers-by' — reflects a real Elizabethan ideology of noble privilege, here carried to absurdity.

anchor_text: You are cock and capon too; and you crow, cock, with your comb on
summary: The Second Lord is speaking in an aside, skewering Cloten's boast that he is 'a cock that nobody can match.' A capon is a castrated rooster — neutered, incapable of fighting or mating — so to call Cloten 'cock and capon too' is to say he is simultaneously all swagger (cock) and impotent (capon). The jest undermines his sexual and martial pretensions in one breath. 'Comb' is a rooster's red crest, a natural phallic emblem in bawdy idiom.

'To crow with your comb on' reduces his bluster to a castrate's strutting: the outward display of a rooster with none of the potency. The joke anticipates the rest of the play, in which Cloten pursues Imogen and threatens violence but is himself killed and unmanned. Capons appear throughout the canon as emblems of unmanliness — see, e.g., Falstaff's 'capon' letters in Henry IV Part 1.

anchor_text: Is it fit I went to look upon him? is there no derogation in't
summary: 'Derogation' means a lessening of rank or dignity — the fear that doing something below one's station would damage one's noble standing. Cloten worries that receiving or meeting a lesser visitor might be a concession unworthy of his status. The Second Lord's double-edged reply — 'You cannot derogate, my lord' — means ostensibly 'nothing could lower your dignity,' but in aside implies 'you have no dignity left to lower.'
detail: The term comes from heraldic and legal usage: an act 'derogatory' to a gentleman's rank was one that could theoretically forfeit his coat of arms. The joke turns on Cloten being too foolish to hear the insult contained in the compliment. His anxiety about status is a running motif: he chafes that others dare not fight him because of his mother's protection, and that even being matched by an opponent would require them to be 'of his rank' — all index of a man whose only claim is his birth.

The glossing of 'derogation' as loss of rank or dignity is accurate, and the double-meaning of the Second Lord's reply ('You cannot derogate') — the surface compliment concealing the insult that Cloten has no dignity left to lose — is directly supported by the full aside at TLN 852-853 ('You are a fool granted; therefore your issues, being foolish, do not derogate'), confirming the sarcasm.

anchor_text: More hateful than the foul expulsion is Of thy dear husband, than that horrid act Of the divorce he'ld make
summary: The Second Lord is listing the threats Imogen endures, and this clause is the most tangled of them. The structure is: '[Cloten is] more hateful than [even] the foul expulsion of thy dear husband is [hateful], [and more hateful] than that horrid act — the divorce he would make.' Cloten's pestering, in other words, is worse than the banishment of Posthumus and worse than the forced annulment Cloten and the Queen are pushing for. 'He'ld' is a contracted form of 'he would.'
detail: The inverted syntax ('hateful...is') and the interrupted comparison ('than...than') are characteristic of the Jacobean Cymbeline's deliberately knotted style, noted by editors since Theobald. Tracking the referents is the difficulty: the two 'than' clauses both modify the original comparative ('more hateful'), and the whole construction is subordinate to the previous line's 'wooer.' The Second Lord's speech here shifts from prose-like list to compressed verse, marking the moment of emotional weight.

The syntactic analysis is sound: the two 'than' clauses both modify 'more hateful,' the antecedent is Cloten-as-wooer, and 'he'ld' as 'he would' is uncontroversial; attributing the knotted style to Cymbeline's broader Jacobean complexity is a mainstream editorial observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: keep unshaked That temple, thy fair mind
summary: The Second Lord closes with a prayer for Imogen, calling her mind a 'temple' — a metaphor that makes her inner virtue a sacred building the heavens must protect from assault. A temple is both a place of worship and something architecturally inviolable; to 'keep it unshaked' is to pray that it stand firm against the battering of Cloten's pursuit, her stepmother's plotting, and her father's misjudgement. The imagery aligns Imogen's chastity and honour with a holy site.
detail: The 'temple' metaphor for the virtuous mind or body is widespread in early modern religious-philosophical writing (compare Paul, 1 Corinthians 3:16-17: 'ye are the temple of God'). Shakespeare applies it here to Imogen's character rather than body, linking her identity as the play's moral centre with something divinely protected. The prayer-like structure of the whole closing speech ('The heavens hold firm... keep unshaked... that thou mayst stand') formally elevates Imogen against the comic degradation of Cloten that has preceded it, establishing the emotional stakes before the bedchamber scene of 2.2.

anchor_text: Our Tarquin thus Did softly press the rushes, ere he waken'd The chastity he wounded
summary: Iachimo compares himself to Tarquin — Sextus Tarquinius, son of Rome's last king — who crept through the rushes strewn on the floor to reach the sleeping Lucrece before assaulting her. 'Press the rushes' means tread lightly on the rushes used as floor-covering. 'The chastity he wounded' means Lucrece's honour, which Tarquin violated. Iachimo is casting his own night-time theft as an act of sexual violation even though he takes only a bracelet.
detail: Shakespeare had told the Tarquin and Lucrece story at length in his narrative poem The Rape of Lucrece (1594), drawing on Livy 1.57-59 and Ovid's Fasti 2.685-852. The precision of the echo is important: Tarquin moved silently through floor-rushes before acting, and Iachimo echoes that stealth exactly ('from the trunk' to the bedside). The parallel frames Iachimo's espionage as moral rape — a crime against Imogen's honour even without physical contact. The same Tarquin figure recurs in Macbeth, where the murderer 'with Tarquin's ravishing strides' approaches the sleeping Duncan (2.1), making stealthy predation at night a recurring emblem of violation. Iachimo's use of 'Our' Tarquin signals a Roman's proprietary pride in the story, undercutting itself: he is invoking a figure who became the cause of Rome's greatest shame — the expulsion of the kings.

anchor_text: Cytherea, How bravely thou becomest thy bed, fresh lily
summary: 'Cytherea' is a poetic name for Venus, the goddess of love and beauty, taken from the island of Cythera (off the southern coast of Greece), where she was worshipped and near which legend said she rose from the sea. Iachimo addresses Imogen as Cytherea — comparing her beauty in sleep to the goddess herself. 'How bravely thou becomest thy bed' means how perfectly, how magnificently you suit your bed.
detail: Venus was born from the sea-foam near Cythera, according to Hesiod's Theogony (191-206) and retold by Ovid in Metamorphoses 4 and Fasti 4. By the Elizabethan period 'Cytherea' was a standard elevated periphrasis for Venus, carrying associations of irresistible, divine beauty. The address is deeply ironic: Iachimo invokes the goddess of love while behaving as a predator, and the comparison aestheticises his violation of Imogen's privacy. The blazon that follows — white against the sheets, ruby lips, the candle leaning toward her eyes — is a voyeur's inventory in the language of Petrarchan praise-poetry, lending Iachimo's crime the decorum of erotic verse. 'Bravely' = finely, magnificently (archaic sense; cf. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'brave').

'Cytherea' as standard Elizabethan periphrasis for Venus is sound, the blazon-as-voyeuristic-inventory reading is mainstream, and the identification of 'bravely' as archaic for 'finely/magnificently' is correct.

anchor_text: O sleep, thou ape of death, lie dull upon her! And be her sense but as a monument, Thus in a chapel lying
summary: 'Ape' here means imitator — sleep is the image or counterfeit of death, which is why it was a classical and Renaissance commonplace to call sleep 'death's brother' or death's copy. Iachimo prays that Imogen stay deep asleep while he works. 'Be her sense but as a monument, / Thus in a chapel lying' means: let her senses (consciousness) be as lifeless as a stone effigy on a tomb — the recumbent stone figures that lay on top of funeral monuments in English churches. Together the images cast Imogen as already dead, which heightens the horror of Iachimo's living gaze.
detail: The 'ape of death' formula derives from the ancient equation of sleep and death: Homer calls Sleep and Death twin brothers (Hypnos and Thanatos, Iliad 14.231), and the Latin formula 'somnus imago mortis' ('sleep is the image of death') was a school commonplace. 'Ape' in Elizabethan English meant an imitator or mimic (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'ape': 'to imitate'); 'monument' in the sense of a carved tomb-effigy is an exact visual reference to the recumbent alabaster or stone figures — often hands folded, eyes closed — found in English parish churches and cathedrals. Iachimo's apostrophe to Sleep (a direct address to a personified abstraction) is an apostrophe, one of the rhetorical figures most associated with theatrical soliloquy. The passage also begins his shift from lust to clinical inventory: once he frames Imogen as a corpse, he can itemize her as evidence.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 14.231 (Hypnos and Thanatos as twin brothers, sleep and death).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 903

'Ape' as imitator, sleep as death's counterfeit, and 'monument' as a recumbent tomb-effigy are all defensible and well-supported Elizabethan readings; the apostrophe identification and the shift-to-clinical-inventory reading are mainstream.

anchor_text: She hath been reading late The tale of Tereus; here the leaf's turn'd down Where Philomel gave up
summary: The 'tale of Tereus' is Ovid's story of the rape of Philomela: Tereus, king of Thrace and husband of Procne, raped her sister Philomela and cut out her tongue so she could not tell anyone; she wove the truth into a tapestry. The sisters took revenge by killing Tereus's son, and all three were transformed into birds — Philomela became the nightingale. Imogen is reading this story at the very moment Iachimo, like Tereus, violates her chamber by night. 'Where Philomel gave up' means the page at which the rape occurs.
detail: Ovid's Metamorphoses 6.412-674 is the source; the story was standard grammar-school Latin and was widely read in Arthur Golding's English translation (1567). The parallel is exact and chilling: a treacherous man invades a sleeping or unguarded woman, exploits her vulnerability, and silences her — Philomela was literally silenced by having her tongue cut out; Imogen will be silenced by the false 'evidence' Iachimo is gathering. The book open at the moment of violation is a theatrical emblem: the story Imogen is reading predicts what is being done to her without her knowledge. Shakespeare uses Philomela's myth for violated women elsewhere — most brutally in Titus Andronicus, where Lavinia, raped and mutilated, points to this very passage in Ovid to identify her attackers.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.412-674 (Golding's English translation, 1567): the rape of Philomela by Tereus, her transformation into the nightingale.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 916

Identification of 'the tale of Tereus' as Ovid's Philomela story (Met. 6) is exact; 'Where Philomel gave up' as the rape passage is the standard reading; the parallel with Iachimo's own violation of Imogen's privacy is a well-established scholarly observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: penetrate her with your fingering
summary: Cloten's instructions to the musicians carry an obvious sexual double meaning. 'Fingering' means both the technique of playing a stringed instrument and sexual touching; 'tongue' in the next line extends the pun. The bawdy is not accidental — Cloten intends to wear Imogen down by any means and his language expresses that intent even as he speaks of music.
detail: The double entendre is sustained across three lines (935-937): 'penetrate ... fingering ... tongue.' On the surface Cloten advises the musicians to play and sing; beneath the surface he is imagining Imogen's body. Shakespeare makes Cloten's coarseness lexically inescapable: every word he uses for the musicians' art doubles as a word for sexual action. The effect establishes that his courtship is essentially coercive — he speaks of seduction the way one speaks of assault. Editors from Malone onward have noted the bawdy.

anchor_text: the lark at heaven's gate sings, And Phoebus 'gins arise
summary: Phoebus (also called Apollo) was the Greek and Roman sun-god, who was said to drive a chariot of fire across the sky each day, watering his horses at celestial springs. 'Gins arise' means 'begins to rise.' The song imagines the sun-god's daily journey commencing at dawn, with horses drinking from the dew ('chaliced flowers') before the day's run.
detail: In classical myth the sun moves because Phoebus Apollo (or Helios, often conflated with him) drives four fire-breathing horses across the heavens from east to west. 'Those springs / On chaliced flowers that lies' are the cup-shaped blooms filled with morning dew, serving as watering-troughs for the solar horses. The image is elegant pastoral, but coming from Cloten it is lightly ironic — he is performing culture he does not feel. 'Heaven's gate' is also a familiar Elizabethan phrase (compare Sidney's 'Lark so singing, sore / His wings aloft, at Heaven's gate he sings') and Shakespeare reuses it in Sonnet 29. Ovid, Metamorphoses 2 (Golding 1567) describes Phoebus's horses and their celestial route.

anchor_text: winking Mary-buds begin To ope their golden eyes
summary: 'Mary-buds' are marigolds — named for the Virgin Mary, whose flower they were. 'Winking' means shut or closed (eyelids not yet open), not slyly watching. The song describes marigolds that close at night and open their yellow-orange faces at sunrise, as if waking like the woman addressed.

anchor_text: horse-hairs and calves'-guts, nor the voice of unpaved eunuch to boot
summary: 'Horse-hairs' are the strings of the bow used on a viol or fiddle; 'calves'-guts' are the gut strings of a lute or viol. An 'eunuch' here means a castrated male singer — boys or men who were castrated before puberty to preserve a high soprano voice. 'Unpaved' means literally 'without paving-stones,' that is, lacking testicles. Cloten is saying that if even the finest music and singing cannot move Imogen, it is a flaw in her ears, not the musicians.

anchor_text: The exile of her minion is too new
summary: 'Minion' here means a favourite or darling — specifically Posthumus, whom Imogen loves and who has just been banished. anchor_text: Who lets go by no vantages that may Prefer you to his daughter

'Prefer' means to advance or promote — the Queen is telling Cloten that Cymbeline uses every opening to forward Cloten's suit with Imogen. The whole speech is the Queen coaching her son in patient, strategic courtship: take every chance, appear devoted, and above all don't give up when she says no.

anchor_text: ambassadors from Rome; The one is Caius Lucius
summary: Caius Lucius is the Roman general and ambassador sent by Caesar Augustus to demand the tribute that Cymbeline has stopped paying. His arrival is the political mainspring of the play's second half: Cymbeline will refuse the tribute, and a Roman invasion will follow. The play's British-Roman war is loosely based on Holinshed's account of the historical king Cunobeline (Cymbeline) and the tribute Britain owed since Julius Caesar's expeditions of 55-54 BC.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) describe a Kymbeline who had been raised at Augustus's court and whose son Guiderius later refused the Roman tribute, provoking invasion. Shakespeare telescopes this into a single reign and uses the tribute-refusal as the political action that mirrors and ultimately resolves the play's personal plots. Lucius himself is courteous and admirable — Cymbeline says 'A worthy fellow, / Albeit he comes on angry purpose now' — which is typical of the play's even-handed treatment of the Romans. See card: ancient-britain-and-the-roman-tribute.

anchor_text: Diana's rangers false themselves, yield up Their deer to the stand o' the stealer
summary: Diana was the goddess of the hunt, and her 'rangers' are her foresters or game-keepers — guardians of chastity as well as of wild animals. Cloten boasts that gold can bribe even Diana's own protectors to betray their charge, letting a poacher ('the stealer') take his 'deer' from their hunting-stand. The pun on 'deer' and 'dear' (a woman) is deliberate: Cloten means he will bribe Imogen's women to help him reach her.
detail: Diana, goddess of the moon, the hunt, and chastity, was the divine emblem of female sexual purity (see card: diana-goddess). Her 'rangers' are simultaneously the game-wardens of a forest and the women who guard Imogen's honour. A 'stand' is a raised platform or fixed station where a hunter waits for deer to be driven past — the 'stealer' takes the prey from the very station where the guardian should be watching. Gold, Cloten argues, corrupts justice itself: it makes the true man killed and saves the thief. The speech is a miniature essay on the corruptive power of money that echoes King Lear's later meditation ('Plate sin with gold, / And the strong lance of justice hurtless breaks,' Lear 4.6).

The hunting-stand / deer / 'dear' pun and 'rangers' as foresters doubling as guardians of chastity are the standard editorial readings; the comparison to King Lear's 'plate sin with gold' is apt as a contextualising parallel, though it is framed as an echo rather than a source-claim.

She is saying that expensive clothing does not make a man noble — a pointed glance at Cloten, who has the rank without the manners. The remark is typical of the scene's satirical treatment of Cloten as a man of mere surface.

summary: The sentence is compressed and ironic: 'one of your great knowing' means 'a person of your vast learning and experience' — Imogen says it sarcastically. anchor_text: Wert thou the son of Jupiter and no more But what thou art besides, thou wert too base To be his groom

Imogen's reference thus has a dramatic double resonance: she invokes the very god who will later intervene on her husband's behalf. anchor_text: The south-fog rot him

anchor_text: abide the change of time, Quake in the present winter's state
summary: Posthumus says he has no way to regain the king's favour except to 'abide' (endure, wait out) the change of time, as one shakes through winter hoping for warmer days. anchor_text: when Julius Caesar Smiled at their lack of skill, but found their courage Worthy his frowning at
summary: Julius Caesar invaded Britain twice (55 and 54 BC) and was surprised to find the Britons fierce fighters despite their primitive military organisation. Posthumus is saying British soldiers have since gained discipline to match their natural courage, making them even more formidable than the warriors Caesar himself respected. This claim is part of a running argument that Rome should not underestimate Britain.
detail: Caesar's own account in the Gallic War describes the Britons' charioteers, their effective guerrilla tactics, and his difficulty controlling the situation despite winning engagements. He extracted a promise of tribute but never permanently conquered the island. Shakespeare knew Caesar's campaigns from Holinshed's Chronicles and probably from direct reading of the Latin or a translation. Posthumus's analysis — courage always there, discipline now added — mirrors a Jacobean-era pride in Britain as a nation that had resisted Rome and ultimately chose, freely, to join its civilisation.

anchor_text: Proud Cleopatra, when she met her Roman, And Cydnus swell'd above the banks
summary: Iachimo describes a tapestry in Imogen's bedchamber depicting Cleopatra's legendary arrival to meet Mark Antony at the river Cydnus in Cilicia (now southern Turkey), when her barge was so magnificent that the crowds emptied the riverbanks to watch. Shakespeare was writing Cymbeline at the same time as Antony and Cleopatra, and the allusion invokes the most famous image of erotic spectacle in the classical world.

The tapestry's subject is not innocent: it associates Imogen's bedchamber with the most renowned seductress in history, which is exactly the atmospheric insinuation Iachimo needs to make Posthumus uneasy, even though Imogen herself is nothing like Cleopatra. The river swelling 'above the banks' — from the press of boats or from civic 'pride' (the river itself swelling with pride at Cleopatra's passage) — is a detail from Plutarch.

anchor_text: Chaste Dian bathing: never saw I figures So likely to report themselves: the cutter Was as another nature, dumb; outwent her
summary: The chimney-piece in Imogen's room is carved with the goddess Diana bathing — the scene in which Actaeon accidentally glimpsed her and was turned into a stag and killed by his own hounds. Diana was the goddess of chastity, so her image above Imogen's fireplace is an emblem of the room's inhabitant. Iachimo praises the sculptor: the figures were so lifelike they seemed about to speak — the carver was 'as another nature, dumb,' meaning a second nature that was only mute.

By choosing this subject for the mantelpiece, Imogen (or whoever furnished the room) placed chastity under Diana's protection. Iachimo, who has himself crept into the room while Imogen slept, is describing the very image that condemns his own intrusion — he is a second Actaeon, a voyeur in Diana's space. The 'cutter' is the stone-carver (a technical term for a sculptor in relief); 'outwent her' means surpassed nature itself.

anchor_text: were two winking Cupids Of silver, each on one foot standing, nicely Depending on their brands
summary: Iachimo describes two silver andirons (fireplace supports) shaped as Cupid figures — the god of love, son of Venus — balancing on one foot and leaning on their 'brands,' meaning their torches. 'Winking' here means eyes half-closed or sleepy. 'Depending' means leaning, balancing. Cupid's torch was one of his standard attributes: love was imagined as a flame kindled by his burning torch as well as by his arrows.

Cupid was most often depicted as a winged, blindfolded or squinting boy with bow and arrows, but his torch — the fire of love — was equally conventional. 'Nicely Depending' means 'delicately balanced' or 'carefully poised.' The detail is significant because fire-implements shaped as Cupids sit directly below the chaste Diana carving on the chimney-piece: the room positions love (Cupid, below, heating) beneath chastity (Diana, above, cooling) — a decorative emblem of Imogen's character, and an ironic comment on Iachimo's errand.

anchor_text: It is a basilisk unto mine eye, Kills me to look on't
summary: The basilisk was a legendary serpent or dragon whose gaze killed instantly. Posthumus, handing over his ring, says looking at it is lethal: it kills him to see the bracelet that proves (he believes) Imogen's infidelity. The image is precise — his own love-token has become a deadly thing that destroys him when he looks at it.
detail: The basilisk appeared in classical natural history (Pliny, Natural History 8.33) as a small serpent that routed other snakes with its hiss and was said to kill by its very sight; Pliny also reports that it scorched grass and burst rocks with its breath. Renaissance writers amplified the legend so that its very glance was lethal. Heraldry used the cockatrice (a basilisk with a cockerel's head) as a standard figure, and the creature is a favourite Shakespearean image for something that destroys by being seen — compare Richard III 1.2 and 3 Henry VI 3.2. The ring that was a love-pledge has been converted by Iachimo's false narrative into evidence of betrayal: to see it now is to see the ruin of Posthumus's marriage.

anchor_text: Let there be no honour Where there is beauty; truth, where semblance; love, Where there's another man
summary: Posthumus delivers a series of parallel 'let there be no X where there is Y' statements — a rhetorical device called anaphora (repeated opening) and chiasmus (reversing logical expectation). The grammar is compressed: he means 'let honour not be expected where beauty exists; let truth not be expected where only appearance is; let love not be expected where a third party is present.' It is a bitter generalisation against women drawn from what he believes is one example.
detail: The rhetorical movement here — from a specific betrayal to a universal law — is the same cognitive error Othello makes after Iago's false proofs. 'Semblance' means outward appearance, seeming rather than reality. The passage ends with a misogynist conclusion ('the vows of women / Of no more bondage be... than they are to their virtues; which is nothing') that the audience knows to be wrong, since Imogen is entirely faithful. The speech is the pivot on which Posthumus's character turns: he will spend the rest of the play in guilt and repentance for this misjudgement.

anchor_text: The cognizance of her incontinency Is this: she hath bought the name of whore thus dearly
summary: 'Cognizance' is a heraldic and legal term meaning a visible badge, token, or proof that identifies something. Posthumus means: this bracelet is the identifying mark — the proof — of Imogen's 'incontinency,' a formal word for sexual unchastity. The sentence is cruelly precise: the love-token she was supposed to guard has become, in his twisted reading, the emblem of her faithlessness.
detail: In heraldry a cognizance (or cognisance) was an emblem worn by a lord's followers to identify their allegiance — a visible sign of belonging. In legal usage it meant an acknowledgement or formal recognition. Posthumus is appropriating the technical vocabulary of proof and identification to declare the bracelet definitive evidence. 'Incontinency' (sexual incontinence, failure of chastity) was the standard euphemism in formal and legal discourse for what he goes on to name plainly.

anchor_text: She hath been colted by him
summary: 'Colted' is a coarse sexual term: to colt a woman meant to mount her as a stallion mounts a mare, i.e., to have intercourse with her. Posthumus, now fully convinced of Imogen's infidelity, uses the most degrading animal metaphor available — reducing her to a mare and Iachimo to a stud horse. The word is otherwise used of young horses or of being tricked, but the sexual sense is dominant here given the context.
detail: The equine sexual vocabulary was available in early modern English: 'colt' (a young, unbroken horse) and 'jade' (a worn-out horse) were both applied to women pejoratively, often to signal male contempt. The phrase is the emotional nadir of Posthumus's rage — he has moved from legal vocabulary ('cognizance') to this raw, animal insult in under ten lines. Editors including the Arden and Oxford note the sexual sense as primary in this context (cf. OED s.v. anchor_text: Spare your arithmetic: never count the turns; Once, and a million!
summary: Posthumus interrupts Iachimo before he can list more sexual 'proofs.' 'Count the turns' means count the number of sexual encounters — 'turn' was a common euphemism for a sexual act. Posthumus's 'Once, and a million!' means: whether she did it once or a million times, the fact is the same — the marriage is destroyed. The arithmetical conceit (spare your arithmetic, count, once vs a million) gives a savage veneer of cool logic to his anguish.
detail: The word 'turn' as a euphemism for a sexual act was current in early modern English (cf. Othello's 'hath the act of shame a thousand times committed,' 5.2). Posthumus refuses to hear the details — not because he disbelieves them but because, in his broken state, the number is irrelevant: infidelity once or infinitely is the same ruin. The grammar of 'Once, and a million!' is deliberately paradoxical: a single act has the weight of uncountable repetitions. The gesture anticipates his final paradox of forgiveness — he will later resolve to pardon her regardless of facts.

anchor_text: I had her here, to tear her limb-meal
summary: 'Limb-meal' means limb from limb, piece by piece — the '-meal' suffix in Shakespeare's period meant 'by portions at a time' (cf. 'inch-meal,' by inches; 'piecemeal,' piece by piece). Posthumus is saying he wishes he could tear Imogen apart limb by limb. The word appears nowhere else in Shakespeare, intensifying the violence of his wish and the extremity of his betrayed rage.
detail: The suffix '-meal' in Elizabethan English derived from Old English '-maelum,' meaning 'by measure / by portion at a time.' It forms adverbs of graduated action: 'piecemeal' (piece by piece), 'inch-meal' (inch by inch — used by Caliban in The Tempest 2.2), 'limb-meal' (limb by limb). The violence of the wish is significant: Posthumus immediately abandons it for the more public humiliation of confronting Imogen at court, and then exits mid-sentence ('I'll do something—'), leaving even that threat unspecified. The open-ended exit is a sign of his psychological collapse.

anchor_text: Quite besides The government of patience! You have won: Let's follow him, and pervert the present wrath
summary: Philario means Posthumus has gone 'quite beside' — entirely beyond — any self-control; 'the government of patience' means the authority or rule of patience, the capacity to govern himself with patience. 'Pervert' here does not mean 'corrupt' but 'divert, turn aside' — Philario wants to redirect Posthumus's rage away from himself before he does something irreversible. The phrase 'beside himself' (meaning out of one's mind with passion) is the idiom behind 'quite besides.'
detail: 'Government' in Shakespeare regularly means self-restraint or self-command — the internal government of one's emotions — not only political rule. 'Pervert' from Latin pervertere meant primarily 'to turn aside, to divert from a course' before narrowing to modern pejorative senses; the Arden editors gloss it as 'avert, turn aside.' Iachimo's cool closing couplet — 'With all my heart' — shows his utter detachment: he has won the wager and Posthumus's destruction is someone else's problem.

anchor_text: some coiner with his tools Made me a counterfeit
summary: Posthumus extends a coinage metaphor across two lines: a 'coiner' is a minter of money, and to be 'stamp'd' is to have the official die pressed onto a coin. He means that his father was absent when he was conceived, so some unknown man ('some coiner') used the tools of sex to produce Posthumus — a counterfeit, a bastard coin bearing a false mark of legitimacy. The metaphor equates paternity with the royal authorization stamped on currency.
detail: Elizabethan monetary language ran deep: coins were 'stamp'd' with the sovereign's image by a die (the 'tools'), and a 'counterfeit' was a forged coin passing as genuine. Posthumus's logic — that a man's legitimacy depends entirely on the woman's fidelity, since no man can verify his own paternity — drives the whole soliloquy and is the period's sharpest anxiety about female sexuality. The image recurs in Shakespeare: in King Lear (1.2) Edmund, also a bastard, toys with the same coinage of legitimacy. Here it triggers Posthumus's misogynist spiral: if Imogen was unfaithful, then he himself might be the product of similar deception.

anchor_text: A pudency so rosy the sweet view on't Might well have warm'd old Saturn
summary: 'Pudency' means modesty or chastity-shame — the blush of a woman who resists a sexual advance. Posthumus is remembering that when he pressed his conjugal rights Imogen refused him with such a rosy, blushing modesty that even 'old Saturn' — the frozen, aged planet-god, a byword for cold and age — could have been warmed by the sight. The compliment sharpens the betrayal: the very shame that looked like proof of her chastity was, he now believes, a performance.
detail: Saturn in classical cosmology was the outermost, slowest, coldest of the planets, and the god presiding over old age and melancholy; 'old Saturn' therefore means ultimate coldness and joylessness. The word 'pudency' (Latin pudicitia, shame, modesty) appears only here and in one other place in the canon (Antony and Cleopatra 1.4); it is a Latinate coinage in English. Posthumus's image inverts: what could have warmed the coldest thing in creation must be the deepest warmth — and he now attributes it to hypocrisy rather than genuine virtue. The passage is among Cymbeline's characteristically tortured late-style constructions.

anchor_text: Like a full-acorn'd boar, a German one, Cried 'O!' and mounted
summary: Posthumus imagines Iachimo seducing Imogen with the speed and animal urgency of a 'full-acorn'd boar' — a boar fattened on acorns and therefore at the peak of rutting energy. 'Mounted' is unambiguous for the sex act. The 'German' qualifier may add a note of foreign boorishness; the German boar was proverbially large and fierce. The fantasy is Posthumus's torment: he pictures Imogen meeting no resistance ('found no opposition / But what he look'd for should oppose') — i.e. the bodily response he believed she lacked.
detail: The boar as an image of male sexual aggression was familiar to Shakespeare's audience: the boar that kills Adonis in Venus and Adonis is charged with erotic menace. 'Full-acorn'd' specifies the highest state of a boar's physical readiness; the redundant 'a German one' slows the verse for emphasis, making the image more brutal, not less. 'Mounted' (to mount an animal: to copulate) is direct sexual vocabulary used without any distancing. The scene asks the audience to watch a husband's imagination furnish a pornographic betrayal that may never have happened — Iachimo's 'evidence' was a bracelet and a birthmark, not an eye-witness account.

anchor_text: The woman's part in me! For there's no motion That tends to vice in man
summary: Posthumus launches a rhetorical catalogue — an anaphora, a repeated hammering of the phrase 'the woman's part' — in which he assigns every human vice to women. 'The woman's part in me' first means a literal anatomical wish: he wants to cut out whatever in him derives from female inheritance. Then it shifts to a broad misogynist claim: lying, flattering, deceiving, lust, revenge, ambition, 'nice longing' (foolish craving), slander, mutability — all hers. 'Nice' here means wanton or foolish, not pleasant.
detail: The device is anaphora: the phrase 'the woman's part' / 'hers' strikes like a hammer across six lines. The speech is the play's darkest moment for Posthumus — he has swallowed Iachimo's fiction whole, and the result is a comprehensive hatred that condemns all women on the evidence of one supposed betrayal. Editors note that the speech also destabilizes him as a character: calling it 'The woman's part in me' implicates himself in what he condemns, since the vices he lists (lying, deceiving, mutability) are exactly what Iachimo practised on him. 'Mutability' — inconstancy, changeability — was an Elizabethan stock charge against women, rooted in Galenic medicine's idea that women were 'cold and moist' and therefore unstable by nature.

anchor_text: Julius Caesar, whose remembrance yet Lives in men's eyes
summary: Caius Lucius is collecting a tribute first owed since Julius Caesar conquered Britain in 55-54 BC. Caesar invaded twice and forced the British king Cassibelan (historically Cassivellaunus) to promise yearly payments to Rome. The play is set in the reign of Augustus, Caesar's successor, and that long-unpaid debt is the war's trigger.
detail: Julius Caesar's Gallic War (Books 4-5) records the two British expeditions and the tribute imposed on the defeated Cassivelaunus. Shakespeare follows Holinshed's Chronicles (1587), which calls the king 'Cassibelan' and credits him with resisting Caesar's full subjugation even while granting tribute. The 'three thousand pounds yearly' (TLN 1338) is Shakespeare's specific figure, not Caesar's; Holinshed and the historical sources give no precise sum. Caius Lucius's role as ambassador demanding arrears places the scene in the early reign of Augustus (roughly the same era as the Nativity, a temporal coincidence the play later exploits).

The Queen's interjection before Lucius has even finished speaking signals the scornful, pre-emptive tone she and Cloten adopt throughout the scene, usurping Cymbeline's reply with a unilateral declaration.

anchor_text: There be many Caesars, Ere such another Julius. Britain is A world by itself
summary: Cloten's boast is a crude form of the rhetorical device called 'diminutio' — belittling a famous name to deflate the opponent's authority. His point: there have been many men called Caesar since Julius, but no one to match him, so the title alone proves nothing. 'Britain is a world by itself' became a famous nationalist slogan: the island's isolation makes it its own self-contained realm, owing nothing to Rome.
detail: The claim that Britain is 'a world by itself' — separated by the sea and therefore exempt from Rome's jurisdiction — was a piece of Jacobean-era island pride. The Queen will develop it into her Neptune's-park speech. Ironically, the sentiment is put in the mouth of the play's most foolish character, Cloten, which undercuts its grandeur even as the argument is taken up by more serious speakers. 'Ere such another Julius' is compressed syntax for 'before there will be [or has been] such another one as Julius.'

anchor_text: natural bravery of your isle, which stands As Neptune's park, ribbed and paled in With rocks unscalable
summary: The Queen describes Britain as Neptune's (the sea-god's) enclosed game-park, 'ribbed and paled in' — the ribs and pales being the wooden posts and rails of a fence, here replaced by unscaleable sea-cliffs and roaring surf. It is a sustained metaphor: the island is a natural fortress, and no fleet can cross it unsunken. 'Paled in' means fenced in with pales (stakes).
detail: The speech is a set-piece of Jacobean island patriotism. Neptune (Roman god of the sea) as the park-owner extends the enclosure metaphor: just as a nobleman's park is walled against trespassers, Britain is walled by the sea-god's own terrain. 'Ribbed' suggests both the bone-like cliff-faces and ship-ribs — the natural ribs that replace any built fortification. Scholars note the speech's resemblance to John of Gaunt's 'sceptred isle' speech in Richard II (2.1), equally celebrating Britain's sea-defences; both are patriotic commonplaces, but the Queen's version is specifically deployed to justify defiance.

anchor_text: made not here his brag Of 'Came' and 'saw' and 'overcame'
summary: The Queen is mocking Julius Caesar's famous boast 'veni, vidi, vici' ('I came, I saw, I conquered'), which he reportedly sent to the Roman Senate after a swift victory in Asia Minor in 47 BC. Her point is that Caesar could not make that boast about Britain — he was twice beaten back and had to sail home in shame.
detail: Suetonius records the phrase 'veni, vidi, vici' as Caesar's message after Zela (47 BC), chosen for its punchy alliteration and brevity (Suetonius, Julius 37). Plutarch also reports it (Life of Caesar 50). The Queen's version — 'Came and saw and overcame' — deliberately translates the Latin into flat, graceless English, stripping the phrase of its rhetorical punch to mock Caesar's failure in Britain. The following lines describe his two failed expeditions (55-54 BC), when storms wrecked his fleet; this is substantially accurate to Caesar's own account in the Gallic War.

sources.name: Suetonius, Julius Caesar

anchor_text: O giglot fortune!--to master Caesar's sword
summary: 'Giglot' (also spelled 'giglet') meant a wanton, giddy, or promiscuous woman — a common term of abuse for a flirt. The outburst is a parenthetical exclamation at Fortune's fickleness.

anchor_text: Caesar's ambition, Which swell'd so much that it did almost stretch The sides o' the world, against all colour
summary: 'Against all colour' means 'without any legal justification, without any appearance of right' — 'colour' in Elizabethan legal usage meant a semblance or pretence of legal right. The phrase modifies the whole previous clause: Caesar's ambition stretched the limits of the world and then, with no lawful ground at all, placed the yoke of tribute on Britain.

Cymbeline is here making the constitutional argument that the tribute was extorted by naked power with no legal basis; the same argument underlies the Britains' refusal throughout the scene. 'The sides o' the world' is hyperbole for the known world's boundaries: an ambition that 'almost stretched the sides' is one that nearly burst the world's frame. The main-clause verb governing 'ambition' is 'Did put the yoke upon 's' (TLN 1384), requiring the reader to hold the relative clause 'which swell'd...' across several lines before reaching the main predicate.

anchor_text: Our ancestor was that Mulmutius which Ordain'd our laws
summary: Mulmutius (or Molmutius) is a legendary pre-Roman king of Britain who, according to Holinshed's Chronicles, gave Britain its first written laws — the 'Mulmutine laws' — and was the first British king to wear a golden crown. Cymbeline invokes him to claim that Britain had its own ancient legal order before Rome arrived, and that restoring it justifies defying the tribute.

Shakespeare had used the same legend in 2 Henry IV (3.1), where Warwick says English rivers were 'lined and interlined with many English ditches' in Mulmutius's time. For a Jacobean audience, the appeal to ancient British law over Roman imperial authority carried resonance in debates about the extent of parliamentary and common-law tradition against royal prerogative.

anchor_text: What false Italian, As poisonous-tongued as handed
summary: Pisanio brands the unknown slanderer as a 'false Italian' — invoking the Elizabethan stock figure of the Italian as charming, eloquent, but treacherous and skilled with poison. 'Poisonous-tongued as handed' means equally dangerous with words and with actual poison (Italy being associated with poisoning).

Webster, Jonson, and Shakespeare repeatedly cast Italian characters as subtle deceivers; Iachimo, who has in fact poisoned Posthumus's mind against Imogen with a fabricated story, is the scene's obvious target, though Pisanio does not yet know his name. The compound 'poisonous-tongued as handed' fuses verbal and physical treachery: as lethal in speech as in deed.
