anchor_text: More goddess-like than wife-like, such assaults As would take in some virtue
summary: Pisanio says Imogen endures Posthumus's false accusation 'more goddess-like than wife-like' — a hyperbole that elevates her constancy above ordinary human steadfastness. 'Such assaults as would take in some virtue' means attacks powerful enough to overwhelm even a genuinely virtuous person.
detail: The figure is a 'praeteritio' of comparison: Pisanio goes beyond the expected praise ('she is a good wife') to a higher category ('she is more than human'). 'Take in' means to capture or overcome, as a military force takes in a town; the metaphor casts Imogen's honour as a fortification under siege. The whole speech (1425-1448) is a soliloquy of shocked loyalty: Pisanio, reading a letter ordering him to murder his mistress, must voice the play's moral reality that Imogen is innocent. His rhetoric — 'goddess-like,' 'more goddess-like than wife-like' — sets the register for how the audience is to understand her throughout.

anchor_text: Art thou a feodary for this act
summary: A 'feodary' (also 'feodary') was a feudal vassal — someone who held land in exchange for service and loyalty to a lord. Here Pisanio asks the letter scornfully whether it is a willing accomplice, a dependent conspirator, in Posthumus's plan to murder Imogen.

The OED records 'fedary/feodary' in Shakespeare in this extended sense (alongside the strictly feudal one); the Folio spelling 'Foedarie' reinforces the legal/feudal sound. Pisanio addresses the letter as an object with agency — a common rhetorical apostrophe — and the choice of 'feodary' accuses the paper of having taken service under an unjust lord (Posthumus's corrupted will). The line's bitterness also shows Pisanio wrestling with his own divided loyalties: his master has become someone he barely recognizes.

anchor_text: O, learn'd indeed were that astronomer That knew the stars as I his characters
summary: In Elizabethan English 'astronomer' often meant an astrologer — someone who read the stars to predict the future. 'Characters' here means handwriting, specifically the letters of Posthumus's script. Imogen says: a stargazer who could read the heavens as well as she can read Posthumus's handwriting would be able to foretell the future.
detail: The distinction between astronomy (the science of celestial bodies) and astrology (divination from them) was less sharp in Shakespeare's day than ours; 'astronomer' commonly carried both meanings. Imogen's conceit maps personal knowledge onto cosmic knowledge: she knows Posthumus's letters so intimately that it is a form of prophecy. 'Characters' for handwriting or letters (from Greek charakter, an engraved mark) is standard in the period — compare Hamlet 1.5: 'I'll wipe away all trivial fond records, / All saws of books, all forms, all pressures past, / That youth and observation copied there.' The logic of the sentence is inverted: 'How learned [that astronomer] would be, if he knew the stars as well as I know Posthumus's handwriting' — a measure of how deeply she has studied him.

anchor_text: Good wax, thy leave. Blest be You bees that make these locks of counsel! Lovers And men in dangerous bonds pray not alike
summary: Imogen breaks the wax seal on Posthumus's letter with a small ceremony. 'Locks of counsel' plays on wax seals locking in secrets. 'Bonds' carries a double meaning: a legal bond (a sealed document, an obligation, a debt-instrument) and the bond of love. She contrasts debtors who dread their bonds with lovers who clasp 'young Cupid's tables' — their love-letters — with joy.
detail: 'Good wax, thy leave' is a polite formula asking permission before breaking the seal, treating the letter as a sacred thing. Bee-wax was used for letter-seals; 'locks of counsel' gives the bees quasi-legal dignity as keepers of private correspondence. The 'bonds' pun is sharp: in law a 'bond' was a sealed written obligation (hence 'men in dangerous bonds' = debtors in legal peril); but for lovers a sealed letter is their bond too, pressed with the same wax, and they pray for good news from it rather than dreading it. 'Cupid's tables' are love-letters or love's record-books (a 'table' was a writing-tablet); to 'clasp' them is both to hold them close and to fasten the clasp of a book. Imogen's mood throughout this passage is breathless anticipation, and the wordplay catches the way she turns every object — wax, bees, seals — into an emblem of love.

anchor_text: I am in Cambria, at Milford-Haven
summary: Cambria is the Latin name for Wales. Milford Haven is a deep-water harbour on the Pembrokeshire coast in southwest Wales, and it becomes the convergence point of the entire plot: Posthumus names it as his location, Imogen races toward it, Pisanio reveals the murder plot there, and the Roman army later lands there.
detail: Milford Haven carried strong Tudor resonance for Shakespeare's audience: it was the port where Henry Tudor (Henry VII, the first Tudor king) landed in 1485 to claim the throne before Bosworth Field, and where his grandson Henry VIII's fleets used the harbour. Placing the play's action there quietly associates Cymbeline's legendary Britain with the Tudor dynasty's founding moment. In the play's mythologized time-scheme, Britain on the edge of war with Rome and Britain on the eve of the Tudor conquest both share this charged western port.

anchor_text: let me bate,--but not like me--yet long'st, But in a fainter kind:--O, not like me; For mine's beyond beyond
summary: The doubled 'beyond beyond' is Imogen's way of saying her longing exceeds any expression — it is past the limit of 'beyond' itself, beyond beyondness. The rhetorical device (repeating a word to multiply its force past its ordinary meaning) is a form of occupatio: she cannot say how great her longing is, so she compounds the word for 'too great to say' to push further still.
detail: The whole passage (1479-1484) is deliberately fractured: Imogen starts a comparison ('Who long'st, like me... but not like me'), catches herself, revises twice, and arrives at the compressed superlative 'mine's beyond beyond' — a doubling that enacts the failure of language to measure love. The syntax mimics an overflowing mind. 'Bate' here means 'diminish' or 'moderate' (to bate = to reduce an amount): she is about to grant that Pisanio longs too, but 'not like me, not in the same degree.' The rhetorical name for the doubled-word device is 'epizeuxis' (immediate repetition for emphasis), but here its purpose is superlative escalation rather than emotional insistence. This kind of extreme-comparison passage is characteristic of Cymbeline's late, knotty verse style.

anchor_text: One score 'twixt sun and sun
summary: 'Score' means twenty; 'twixt sun and sun' means from sunrise to sunset — one day's journey. Pisanio is saying a reasonable traveller can manage twenty miles a day on horseback. 'Madam, 's enough for you' suggests the distance is about right for a woman of rank, though he mutters aside that it is in fact too far.

'Sun and sun' for 'day' is common in the period; compare 'from sun to sun' in Macbeth. The practical geography matters: Milford Haven in west Wales was approximately 200 miles from London by the roads of Shakespeare's day — a ten-day journey at this rate. Imogen's eagerness ('why may not I glide thither in a day?' 1.477) sets her impatience against Pisanio's care for what is physically possible.

anchor_text: A riding-suit, no costlier than would fit A franklin's housewife
summary: A 'franklin' was a free landowner of the middling sort — above a yeoman but below a gentleman — roughly what we would call a prosperous farmer or country squire. Imogen asks for travel clothes plain enough for a franklin's wife so that she can pass unnoticed on the road. The detail signals the start of her disguise: she needs to stop looking like a princess.
detail: The word derives from medieval Latin 'francalanus' (a free-holding tenant); Chaucer's Franklin in The Canterbury Tales is the type. By Elizabethan times a franklin occupied a social rung just below the gentry but well above labourers. Imogen's choice of this figure is precise: not so poor as to attract pity or suspicion, not so rich as to draw attention or require a retinue. This is the first practical step toward becoming the page 'Fidele,' the disguise she will adopt in Wales. 'Housewife' (pronounced 'hussif') simply means the mistress of a household at this social level; it carries no reproach.

anchor_text: Stoop, boys; this gate Instructs you how to adore the heavens
summary: Belarius turns a practical inconvenience — the cave mouth is so low you must bow to enter — into a moral emblem: the humble door teaches reverence that the high arched gates of kings' palaces do not. The juxtaposition of the cave with 'the gates of monarchs' (TLN 1516) drives home the scene's argument that the wild life is spiritually nobler than court life.

anchor_text: perceive me like a crow, That it is place which lessens and sets off
summary: Belarius uses the optical fact that distance makes him look as small as a crow — just as he will look tiny from the hilltop — to launch a maxim: 'place' (rank, position) creates the illusion of importance, making great men look large or small depending on where you stand relative to them. Seeing him shrunk to a crow's size, the boys should remember that courtly greatness is a trick of perspective, not a mark of true worth.

'Sets off' means 'displays to advantage' — place both makes great men seem less (from far off) and sets them off as imposing (when close). The figure is a sceptical commonplace about court life: cf. anchor_text: sharded beetle in a safer hold Than is the full-wing'd eagle

Some editors distinguish 'shard-borne' (carried by its wing-cases) from 'sharded' (having shards), but both refer to the dung-beetle's armour. The eagle was the bird of Jupiter and the standard of Rome, so choosing an eagle as the emblem of dangerous eminence is apt in a play whose Roman war is gathering.

summary: 'Attending for a cheque' means waiting at court (as a servant or retainer) only to receive a rebuke. anchor_text: gain the cap of him that makes 'em fine, Yet keeps his book uncross'd
summary: Courtiers who dress in expensive unpaid-for silk 'gain the cap' (earn the respectful bow) of the tailor who dresses them on credit — and yet leave the tailor's account-book 'uncross'd,' meaning the debt never gets a line drawn through it and so is never settled. The detail is sharply topical: complaints about courtiers running up unpayable debts to haberdashers and tailors are a commonplace of Elizabethan satirical literature.

anchor_text: we, poor unfledged, Have never wing'd from view o' the nest
summary: Guiderius answers Belarius's praise of the outdoor life with a sharp comeback: 'You speak from experience — but we have none. We are unfledged birds who have never left the nest.' 'Unfledged' means a young bird that has not yet grown the feathers needed to fly; metaphorically it means inexperienced, ignorant of the world outside. The bird-extended metaphor carries through Arviragus's complaint two lines later ('Our valour is to chase what flies; our cage / We make a quire,' TLN 1557-1558).

It is an elegant subversion of Belarius's praise — the very natural imagery he uses to celebrate the outdoor life (the beetle, the eagle) is turned back on him to reveal its limitations: untested birds cannot judge whether nest or flight is better.

anchor_text: our cage We make a quire, as doth the prison'd bird, And sing our bondage freely
summary: A 'quire' (the usual Elizabethan spelling of 'choir') is a group of singers. Arviragus says their cave is a cage in which, like a caged bird, they sing — but the singing is itself a kind of bondage. 'Sing our bondage freely' means we freely and willingly express the very captivity that confines us, because we know nothing else. The image is bleaker than it first sounds: the cheerfulness of the captive bird only proves how thoroughly it has accepted its prison.

Arviragus's point is the boys have been so conditioned by the cave that they have come to ornament their own imprisonment. Shakespeare returns to captive birds as images of constrained nature: Ophelia is a 'green girl' kept like a bird 'in a cage' (Hamlet 1.3); Imogen herself will later be described in similar terms.

anchor_text: I as a tree Whose boughs did bend with fruit: but in one night, A storm or robbery, call it what you will, Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my leaves, And left me bare to weather
summary: Belarius describes his sudden disgrace with an extended metaphor: he was once a fruit-laden tree ('boughs did bend with fruit'), but a single night's 'storm or robbery' stripped him of everything — fruit, then leaves — and left the bare trunk exposed. anchor_text: How hard it is to hide the sparks of nature! These boys know little they are sons to the king
summary: In this soliloquy, Belarius reveals the play's central secret to the audience: the boys are actually King Cymbeline's stolen sons, Guiderius and Arviragus. 'Sparks of nature' means the innate signs of noble or royal blood — natural gifts of spirit, courage, and bearing — that keep showing through despite the boys' rough upbringing. The idea that royal blood cannot be suppressed by humble circumstances is a central premise of Elizabethan romances.

The reverse formulation (that mere birth without virtue is nothing) was equally standard. Cymbeline plays both sides: the boys are innately princely, but Belarius has also trained them in virtue and courage. Their instinctive martial ardour and the way Guiderius 'sweats' and 'strains his young nerves' re-enacting Belarius's war stories (TLN 1607-1613) are dramatic proof of the doctrine in action.

anchor_text: their thoughts do hit The roofs of palaces, and nature prompts them In simple and low things to prince it much Beyond the trick of others
summary: 'To prince it' is to act or carry themselves like a prince — the verb 'to prince' means to behave with the natural authority and bearing of royalty. 'Beyond the trick of others' means beyond what ordinary people do by habit or practice ('trick' = characteristic manner or habit). The image of 'thoughts hitting the roofs of palaces' from inside a cave captures visually the contrast between the boys' circumstances and their spiritual ceiling.

anchor_text: ne'er long'd my mother so
summary: The syntax inverts the modern word order: 'ne'er long'd my mother so / To see me first, as I have now' means 'my mother never longed to first see me [at my birth] as much as I now long [to see Posthumus].' The parallel between a mother's longing to see her newborn and a wife's longing to see a husband she has been driven from heightens the intimacy of the reunion Imogen expects — and makes the next turn (the murder letter) the more devastating.

anchor_text: drug-damn'd Italy hath out-craftied him
summary: Elizabethan and Jacobean England stereotyped Italy as a land of poison, scheming, and sophisticated deceit; 'drug-damn'd' concentrates these associations (Italy is 'damned' by poisoners and manipulators). Imogen assumes Posthumus has been tricked or corrupted by Italian villainy — a reasonable inference, since Iachimo is precisely such an Italian schemer.

Roger Ascham's The Schoolmaster (1570) had warned against 'Italianate English' men corrupted by Italian travel. Imogen's intuition is also correct: it is Iachimo, the Italian, who has poisoned Posthumus's mind.

anchor_text: thou art the pandar to her dishonour
summary: A 'pandar' (or pander) is a go-between who facilitates sexual transgression — someone who procures partners for illicit activity. Posthumus's letter warns that if Pisanio refuses to kill Imogen and instead lets her live in supposed adultery, he becomes the enabler of her dishonor. The word derives from Pandarus, the procurer in the Troy legend.

By Shakespeare's day 'pander' or 'pandar' could mean either the active arranger or the passive enabler of vice. Shakespeare uses the word both ways: Pandarus himself appears in Troilus and Cressida, and the noun recurs in Hamlet ('reason panders will,' 3.4). The letter's logic is perverse — Pisanio will become the 'pandar' to Imogen's alleged whoredom if he does not end it by killing her.

summary: A 'jay' was slang for a loose woman or a flashy, showy creature (the bird's gaudy plumage suggested cheap display). anchor_text: like false Aeneas, / Were in his time thought false, and Sinon's weeping
summary: Imogen draws on two figures from the fall of Troy: Aeneas, branded 'false' by some ancient and medieval tradition as a traitor to Troy (he survived while the city burned), and Sinon, the Greek who wept convincingly to make the Trojans drag the wooden horse inside the walls. Both men used apparent honesty to deceive — so, Imogen says, honest Pisanio can hardly expect to be believed now that Posthumus has made all good-seeming men look treacherous.
detail: The tradition of 'false Aeneas' comes partly from medieval treatments of the Troy story (Lydgate, Guido delle Colonne's Historia Destructionis Troiae) in which Aeneas was said to have made a secret deal with the Greeks to save himself, making him a traitor rather than a pious son. Virgil's Aeneid is the counter-tradition that exonerates him. Sinon is a Greek soldier who, feigning desertion and weeping convincingly, persuaded the Trojans to accept the wooden horse (Virgil, Aeneid 2.57-194); his name became a byword for lying through false tears. Imogen's point is about contamination: because Posthumus (her 'true' Aeneas) has proved false, all sincere men will henceforth seem untrustworthy — the honest Pisanio falls under suspicion along with everyone else.

anchor_text: Wilt lay the leaven on all proper men; / Goodly and gallant shall be false and perjured
summary: 'Leaven' is the yeast that makes dough rise but that also, in biblical usage, means a corrupting or spreading influence. To 'lay the leaven on' all proper (handsome, worthy) men means to taint them all with the same suspicion of treachery. Because Posthumus looked so virtuous and proved false, no virtuous-looking man can be trusted.
detail: In the New Testament 'leaven' is repeatedly used as a figure for a small corruption that spreads through a whole mass — 'a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump' (Galatians 5:9, Geneva 1599; cf. 1 Corinthians 5:6). Jesus warns his disciples to 'beware of the leaven of the Pharisees' (Matthew 16:6, Geneva 1599), meaning hypocrisy. Imogen's metaphor is apt: Posthumus's concealed villainy, once revealed, spreads backward through all good appearances. 'Proper' means handsome and of good bearing; 'gallant' means splendidly dressed and honourable-seeming.

The biblical 'leaven as spreading corruption' sense (Galatians 5:9, 1 Corinthians 5:6) is well-established and directly apt to Imogen's point that Posthumus's one treachery taints all good-seeming men; no over-reading.

anchor_text: Against self-slaughter / There is a prohibition so divine / That cravens my weak hand
summary: Imogen wants to die but is held back by the Christian prohibition against suicide — to kill oneself was 'self-slaughter,' a mortal sin against God, who alone holds the right to take life. 'Cravens my weak hand' means makes my hand a coward (craven means cowardly; here used as a verb, 'to craven' = to make cowardly).
detail: The Sixth Commandment ('Thou shalt not kill,' Exodus 20:13, Geneva 1599) was understood in Elizabethan theology to forbid self-killing as well as murder, and the Church refused Christian burial to suicides. Hamlet uses almost the same reasoning: 'Or that the Everlasting had not fix'd / His canon 'gainst self-slaughter' (1.2). The word 'divine' explicitly roots the prohibition in God's authority. 'Cravens' as a verb is rare but attested: to make into a craven (coward) — Imogen says the divine law makes her hand too fearful to act.

The Christian prohibition on suicide rooted in the Sixth Commandment and the Hamlet parallel ('the Everlasting's canon 'gainst self-slaughter,' 1.2) are both accurate and the mainstream gloss; 'cravens' as a verb (to make cowardly) is OED-attested.

anchor_text: The scriptures of the loyal Leonatus, / All turn'd to heresy? Away, away, / Corrupters of my faith! you shall no more / Be stomachers to my heart
summary: Imogen turns to Posthumus's love-letters, which she has been keeping against her breast. She calls them her 'scriptures' (sacred texts), now 'turned to heresy' (false doctrine). 'Stomachers' were decorative chest-pieces women wore over the front of their bodices; the letters have been her heart's armor. Now she tears them away.
detail: A stomacher was a triangular piece of stiff decorated fabric worn over a woman's chest and stomach, inside or outside the bodice — a literal covering of the heart. Imogen has kept Posthumus's letters against her breast as if they were sacred scripture, a faith she built her life on. The religious vocabulary — scriptures, heresy, faith, corrupters — carries strong resonance: the betrayal is compared to a spiritual apostasy, not merely a personal betrayal. Tearing off the letters as 'stomachers' enacts the breaking of the faith physically, and the following lines develop the theology of betrayal: the traitor stands 'in worse case of woe' than the betrayed.

anchor_text: when thou shalt be disedged by her / That now thou tirest on, how thy memory / Will then be pang'd by me
summary: 'Disedged' means blunted, made dull — the edge (keenness of appetite or desire) worn off. 'Tirest on' uses a falconry term: a hawk 'tires' when it tears and feeds ravenously at its prey. Imogen predicts that when Posthumus's lust for his new Italian mistress is spent and blunted, his memory of the true, faithful wife he threw away will cause him anguish.
detail: Both words are metaphors of appetite: 'disedge' (to lose one's edge, to become blunt; OED s.v. 'disedge') treats desire as a blade worn down by use; 'tire' is a technical hawking term for the way a falcon tears at and feeds on flesh (Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'tire'). Together they paint Posthumus in the grip of voracious new lust that will inevitably exhaust itself. 'Pang'd' means stabbed with regret. The compressed grammar 'disedged by her / That now thou tirest on' is a characteristically dense late-Shakespeare construction.

anchor_text: To be unbent when thou hast ta'en thy stand, / The elected deer before thee
summary: The image is from deer hunting. A hunter 'takes his stand' (waits at a fixed post) and 'bends' his bow when the targeted ('elected') deer comes into range. To be 'unbent' at that moment — to lower the bow without shooting — is to let the moment go to waste. Imogen accuses Pisanio of leading her all this way, only to refuse the kill at the very moment she stood before him.
detail: Tudor deer hunts were often 'drive' hunts in which archers stood at prearranged stations ('stands') while beaters drove the deer toward them; they would single out ('elect') their target animal and draw ('bend') their bows as it passed. To be 'unbent' at the moment of the elected deer's approach would be a conspicuous failure. The hunting metaphor casts Imogen herself as the hunted animal — willing victim — and Pisanio as the hunter who cannot bring himself to loose the arrow.

anchor_text: mine ear / Therein false struck, can take no greater wound, / Nor tent to bottom that
summary: 'Tent' here is a surgical term: a tent was a roll of cloth or lint inserted into a wound to keep it open and prevent it from closing before it healed from the inside. 'To tent to bottom that' means to probe that wound all the way to the bottom, to sound its full depth. Imogen says her ear has been so thoroughly wounded by the accusation of being a strumpet that nothing worse can reach it.
detail: The medical use of 'tent' as a wound-probe or plug was standard early modern English (OED s.v. 'tent' n.2, a surgical tent or tent-pin; v., to probe a wound with a tent). The phrase 'tent to bottom' suggests probing to the very floor of the wound cavity. Shakespeare uses the medical sense elsewhere: in Troilus and Cressida Ulysses says Achilles' pride 'is a canker, and it must be tented' (2.3). The compressed syntax 'Nor tent to bottom that' means 'nor probe [so as] to reach the bottom of that wound.' 'False struck' means wrongly or dishonestly struck.

anchor_text: I' the world's volume / Our Britain seems as of it, but not in 't; / In a great pool a swan's nest
summary: Imogen argues against treating Britain as the whole world: in 'the world's volume' (the great book of the world, or the entire globe), Britain is merely a part of it, not the whole — like a swan's nest in a vast pool. The image rejects her father's court as the only possible home and opens her mind to Pisanio's plan.
detail: The 'world's volume' metaphor imagines the globe as a great written book, with Britain as a single page or element in it — 'seems as of it' (seems to be part of the book), 'but not in 't' (but is not the whole). The swan's-nest simile diminishes Britain further: a swan's nest is a tiny, thatched float in a large pool, built on the water and subject to its currents. The exchange is a turning point: Imogen's refusal to return to court (she will never 'bide' there) opens the door to Pisanio's plan. The speech also draws on the Jacobean commonplace of Britain as an island-world, which the play both celebrates and complicates.

The 'world's volume' as a book-of-the-world metaphor is plausible, but the annotation adds a 'Jacobean commonplace of Britain as island-world' and implies the swan's-nest simile 'diminishes' Britain in a politically pointed way toward James I; the simile reads more simply as Imogen making a rhetorical argument that the world is large and she need not stay home, and the James-I-island-world reading imports a topical resonance not clearly warranted by this exchange.

anchor_text: The ambassador, / Lucius the Roman, comes to Milford-Haven
summary: Caius Lucius is the Roman general and ambassador sent to collect Britain's overdue tribute to Rome. His arrival at Milford Haven — the great harbour in west Wales — is the historical hinge of the plot: Britain has refused Rome's tribute, and Lucius is about to demand war. Pisanio sees the chance to send Imogen to Rome disguised in his service.
detail: Milford Haven had a particular resonance for Jacobean audiences: it was the harbour where Henry Tudor landed in 1485 to win the English crown at Bosworth, founding the Tudor dynasty that James I claimed to continue. Shakespeare's insistence on Milford — used almost as a talisman throughout the play — ties legendary ancient Britain to Tudor-Stuart dynastic memory. Lucius commands the invading Roman force later in the play, but here his function is purely diplomatic: he carries the Senate's demand and Cymbeline's refusal of the tribute 'left by mighty Caesar' will trigger the war.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1790

anchor_text: change / Command into obedience: fear and niceness-- / The handmaids of all women
summary: 'Niceness' here means fastidiousness, delicacy, or over-refined modesty — the quality of being too careful about propriety. Pisanio says Imogen must abandon her princess's authority ('command') for a servant's obedience, and replace womanly 'fear and niceness' with a 'waggish courage' (bold, irreverent bravery). The speech outlines what a male disguise requires.
detail: In Elizabethan usage 'nice' and 'niceness' most commonly meant over-particular, scrupulous to the point of fussiness — about conduct, appearances, or propriety (OED s.v. 'nice,' senses 5-7). Pisanio lists 'fear and niceness' as the defining female 'handmaids' — attendants, characteristic qualities — that Imogen must discard. The disguise plan is both practical and psychologically precise: to pass as a boy-page Imogen must shed rank, feminine modesty, and caution, and adopt the 'waggish' (playful, impudent) quickness of a young male servant. 'Quarrelous as the weasel' — the weasel was proverbially quick-tempered and aggressive.

anchor_text: the greedy touch / Of common-kissing Titan, and forget / Your laboursome and dainty trims, wherein / You made great Juno angry
summary: 'Titan' is the sun-god (Helios, son of the Titan Hyperion), whose rays touch ('kiss') everyone without distinction — hence 'common-kissing,' the democratizing sun that weathers and tans all faces alike. Imogen's delicate ('dainty') dress and elaborate ('laboursome') grooming once rivalled the queen of the gods herself: Pisanio says she dressed so magnificently she made Juno envious.
detail: The sun as 'Titan' draws on Ovid (Metamorphoses 4.192, 'Hyperione natus,' son of Hyperion; cf. the play's close relative Pericles, where Thaisa is compared to the sun). 'Common-kissing' condenses the idea that outdoor labor exposes the disguised Imogen to sunburn, which will tan her and help her pass as a boy-page. The Juno comparison is both flattering and apt: in the play's mythology Juno presides over marriage, and Imogen's elaborate dress signals her status as a princess and wife. Pisanio's point is that she must abandon all that splendor. The passage also quietly points toward the Act 4.1 betrothal masque where Juno descends to bless union — Imogen's abandoned finery is the negative image of that divine ceremony.

anchor_text: Lest, being miss'd, I be suspected of / Your carriage from the court
summary: 'Carriage' here means the act of carrying off or conveying — Pisanio fears he will be suspected of having spirited Imogen away from the court. The word does not mean a wheeled vehicle in this sense but the abstract noun from 'carry.'
detail: This sense of 'carriage' as the act of conveying or transporting something (or someone) is common in Shakespeare; it is distinct from both the sense of bodily bearing or posture (also common) and the later sense of a horse-drawn vehicle. Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'carriage') distinguishes several senses; this is his sense 2: 'the act of carrying away.' Pisanio risks his life by disobeying his master's order to kill Imogen — and risks it again if the court notices her absence and connects it to him.

anchor_text: Here is a box; I had it from the queen: / What's in't is precious; if you are sick at sea, / Or stomach-qualm'd at land, a dram of this / Will drive away distemper
summary: Pisanio gives Imogen a small box of medicine provided by the Queen, believing it is a powerful remedy for seasickness and illness. The audience knows what Pisanio does not: the Queen obtained this 'medicine' from the physician Cornelius believing it was a deadly poison; Cornelius, suspecting her purpose, gave her instead a drug that induces a death-like sleep. This box will cause Imogen's apparent death in Act 4.
detail: The box is introduced here as a minor act of care but it is the play's most dangerous prop. The audience has watched the Queen obtain what she thought was poison (1.5), and watched Cornelius substitute a sleeping-draft for safety. Pisanio knows only the Queen's assurance that it is a remedy; he passes on both the box and that assurance in good faith. 'Stomach-qualm'd' means suffering from nausea (qualmish = sick at the stomach); 'dram' is a small unit of weight used by apothecaries, here meaning a small dose; 'distemper' means any disorder or illness. The dramatic irony of this scene pivots on the gap between Pisanio's genuine care and the lethal object he hands Imogen.

anchor_text: My emperor hath wrote, I must from hence
summary: 'Hath wrote' is the Elizabethan past tense for 'has written.' The modern form would be 'has written.' In Shakespeare's grammar, the past participle of 'write' could still be 'wrote' rather than 'written,' an older form that survived into the seventeenth century.
detail: Lucius is explaining that he has received imperial orders recalling him from Britain. The archaic past-participle form 'wrote' occurs throughout Shakespeare alongside 'written'; the distinction was not yet fixed in Elizabethan usage. Compare 2 Henry IV 4.1 ('the king hath wrote himself') and Twelfth Night 3.4 ('she hath sent me a letter').

anchor_text: Will not endure his yoke; and for ourself
summary: The 'yoke' Cymbeline refuses is the annual tribute owed to Rome since Julius Caesar's invasion of Britain in 55-54 BC. His phrase 'for ourself / To show less sovereignty than they' means: if his own subjects will not bend to Rome, he as king cannot appear less resolute than they are. The tribute dispute is the play's political engine.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) narrate that the real Cunobeline (Shakespeare's Cymbeline) ruled in the reign of Augustus and that Britain owed tribute from Caesar's expeditions. The Queen's nationalist speech in 3.1 ('Britain's a world by itself') has already inflamed Cymbeline against Rome; this farewell to Lucius is the formal break. Shakespeare's note that 'our subjects will not endure it' lets Cymbeline frame his defiance as responsiveness to popular will, a subtle political gloss on the historical claim.

anchor_text: A conduct over-land to Milford-Haven
summary: A 'conduct' is a safe escort — an armed guard to travel with. Lucius asks for protection on his overland journey to Milford Haven, the great harbour in west Wales, where he will sail back to Rome. Milford Haven is the destination nearly every character in this play converges on, and its name carried a resonance for Jacobean audiences as the landing-place of Henry Tudor in 1485.
detail: The word 'conduct' in the sense of an escorting party (from Latin conductus) was standard diplomatic usage; compare Richard II 1.3 ('A careful father... Hath sent his present here'). Cymbeline's instruction at TLN 1862-1863 — 'The due of honour in no point omit' — ensures Lucius receives full ceremonial escort even as Britain declares him an enemy. The courteous farewell underscores the play's theme that the war between Britain and Rome is political, not personal.

anchor_text: Receive it friendly; but from this time forth
summary: Cloten is shaking hands with Lucius ('Receive it friendly') while simultaneously declaring war: 'but from this time forth / I wear it as your enemy.' The antithesis is pointed — the handshake is performed with one meaning and instantly redefined. 'It' refers to his hand; 'wear it' means 'carry or bear it,' extending the metaphor of the hand-as-weapon to be carried against Rome.
detail: The sequence compresses a courtly farewell gesture into a declaration of hostility: Cloten shakes hands as politeness demands, then immediately uses that same physical gesture as the occasion for announcing enmity. The syntax of 'but from this time forth I wear it' reads oddly — 'wear it' (wear my hand) is an unusual idiom, though Schmidt notes 'wear' in the sense of 'bear or carry' in military contexts (see Macbeth 1.2 'brave Macbeth... like valour's minion'). Lucius's reply ('the event / Is yet to name the winner') is civil and leaves the outcome open.

anchor_text: It fits us therefore ripely
summary: 'Fits us ripely' means 'suits us at exactly the right moment' — 'ripely' in the sense of 'opportunely' or 'at a mature point.' Cymbeline is saying that the war preparations should be made now, because events have reached a natural crisis-point, like fruit that is ripe and ready.
detail: The adverb 'ripely' (opportunely, at just the right time) is found in a few other Shakespeare passages — compare Hamlet 3.3 'when he is drunk asleep, or in his rage, / Or in the incestuous pleasure of his bed — / At game a-swearing, or about some act / That has no relish of salvation in't' (suggesting missed opportunity); and Macbeth 1.3 'a borrowing dulness.' The agricultural metaphor of ripeness for exactly-timed political action is characteristic of Shakespeare: compare 'There is a tide in the affairs of men' (Julius Caesar 4.3) and Gloucester's 'ripeness is all' (King Lear 5.2). Cymbeline's confidence (TLN 1884 'our expectation that it would be thus / Hath made us forward') shows he has been preparing precisely for this moment.

anchor_text: Will soon be drawn to head, from whence he moves
summary: 'Drawn to head' means 'gathered together into a fighting force' — 'head' is a military term for a body of troops mustered for action. Cymbeline says the Roman forces currently in Gaul (France) will soon be concentrated into an army from which Lucius will launch the invasion of Britain.
detail: In military language a 'head' of war (or 'a head') means a formed body of troops ready for action, equivalent to 'raising a force.' Compare 1 Henry IV 4.1 ('all furnish'd, all in arms; / All plumed like estridges') and 2 Henry IV Induction ('making many fish of one;... and drawing a head'). Cymbeline speaks as a competent strategist here: the information that Lucius has already 'wrote to the emperor' (TLN 1876) means Roman preparation is in train, and Cymbeline intends to match it.

'Drawn to head' as military muster is the standard meaning and correctly identified; the context (Gallia, Roman forces) confirms the reading.

anchor_text: hath not appear'd / Before the Roman, nor to us hath tender'd / The duty of the day
summary: 'Tender'd' means 'offered' or 'presented' — it is a formal word for presenting something due (as in 'tendering a payment'). 'The duty of the day' is her daily formal attendance on the king, a court obligation. Cymbeline is angered that Imogen has not appeared before the Roman ambassador and has not performed the standard morning greeting owed by a royal daughter to her father.
detail: 'Tender' as a verb meaning 'to present, offer, or proffer something that is owed' appears frequently in Shakespeare in legal and financial contexts (compare Merchant of Venice 1.3 'I'll tender it'; Hamlet 1.3 'Do not believe his vows; for they are brokers, / Not of that dye which their investments show'). The court protocol of 'the duty of the day' (a formal morning attendance) was a real Tudor convention. Imogen's absence is technically disobedience to the obligations of her rank, which is why Cymbeline calls it 'contempt' (TLN 1900) — the language is quasi-legal.

anchor_text: We have been too slight in sufferance
summary: 'Sufferance' here means 'tolerance' or 'forbearance' — allowing something to continue without punishment. Cymbeline says he has been too lenient ('too slight') in permitting Imogen's defiance. The phrase is a self-criticism: he should have acted sooner.
detail: 'Sufferance' in the sense of 'passive permission; tolerance of what one has the power to prevent' is common Elizabethan usage: compare Merchant of Venice 1.3 ('sufferance is the badge of all our tribe') and Hamlet 3.1 ('the whips and scorns of time, / The oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contumely... and the spurns / That patient merit of the unworthy takes'). 'Slight' as an adjective meaning 'light, not serious enough' is a second archaic usage in the same phrase; 'too slight in sufferance' = 'too light-handed in our tolerance.' Together the phrase captures the king's recognition that he has let a situation drift.

anchor_text: she's a lady / So tender of rebukes that words are strokes / And strokes death to her
summary: The Queen is using a graduated series — words, then strokes, then death — to argue that Imogen is so sensitive that harsh speech would itself be violence. The rhetorical figure is a climax (a chain in which each term is more extreme than the last), here used hypocritically: the Queen is protecting her stepdaughter from Cymbeline's wrath not out of care but to buy time while Imogen is absent.
detail: The rhetorical device of climax (Greek: 'ladder') chains comparisons in ascending intensity. Here: words = strokes; strokes = death. The Queen's speech at TLN 1892-1898 is an example of dramatic irony — she has just soliloquised (TLN 1918-1927) that she hopes Pisanio has swallowed the drug she gave him, and that Imogen has either despaired or fled to her ruin. Her 'forbear sharp speeches to her' is therefore a performance, not sympathy. Shakespeare uses false-protector figures who deploy hyperbolic tenderness as a screen — compare Claudius's theatrical grief in Hamlet 1.2.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1896

Identifying the device as rhetorical climax (words → strokes → death) is correct, and reading the Queen's speech as hypocritical false-protection — given the audience has already seen her soliloquy at TLN 1918-1927 — is the mainstream dramatic-irony interpretation.

anchor_text: She pray'd me to excuse her keeping close, / Whereto constrain'd by her infirmity
summary: 'Keeping close' means staying confined to her rooms, not coming out in public. 'Constrain'd by her infirmity' means forced to do so by her illness. The Queen claims Imogen asked her to pass on an excuse for staying in her chamber, citing illness — a cover story the audience knows is false.
detail: 'Close' as an adverb or adjective meaning 'confined to one place, shut away from public view' is used throughout Shakespeare: compare Much Ado About Nothing 2.3 'Have you observed him since she went? ... I do but stay till your marriage be consummate, and then go I toward Arragon'; and the 'close' conspirators of Julius Caesar 2.1. 'Infirmity' for 'illness' is standard: compare Othello 2.3 ('for my particular grief / Is of so flood-gate and o'erbearing nature / That it engluts and swallows other sorrows'). The Queen adds at TLN 1909-1910 that 'our great court / Made me to blame in memory' — she forgot to pass on the message — a further excuse that shows the facility of her lying.

anchor_text: He hath a drug of mine; I pray his absence / Proceed by swallowing that, for he believes / It is a thing most precious
summary: The Queen gave Pisanio a drug she claimed was a valuable medicine — but which she believes is poison. She is hoping he has taken it and died, so that his absence from court is permanent. The drug is actually the soporific that Cornelius secretly substituted for her poison, and it will later counterfeit death in Imogen who drinks it in 4.2.
detail: The drug plot is set up in Act 1 Scene 5, where the Queen obtains what she thinks is a lethal potion from Cornelius. Cornelius, suspicious, gives her instead a drug that mimics death ('a certain stuff, which being ta'en, / Would ... look like death; and in some sixteen hours / After... revive,' 5.5). The Queen now hopes that Pisanio — loyal to Posthumus and therefore an obstacle to her plans — has been killed. The line 'he believes / It is a thing most precious' establishes how the deception worked: she presented it to him as a rare medicine. This scene confirms that she intends murder, not mere incapacitation, making her the play's most calculating villain.

anchor_text: To death or to dishonour; and my end / Can make good use of either: she being down, / I have the placing of the British crown
summary: In this aside the Queen reveals her plan openly: if Imogen is dead, or publicly disgraced, then the Queen's son Cloten can be married to whoever holds the crown, and the Queen can control who becomes the next ruler of Britain. 'She being down' means Imogen being removed from the succession — either killed or dishonoured. 'The placing of the British crown' is pure usurpation-by-proxy.
detail: The Queen's calculation is that Imogen is Cymbeline's only acknowledged heir; if Imogen is eliminated, the crown would pass as Cymbeline directed — and the Queen means to be the power behind that direction. The phrase 'make good use of either' is chilling in its political detachment: death and dishonour are merely alternative instruments toward the same end. The speech crystallises her role as the play's calculating political villain (distinct from Iachimo's personal wager-driven villainy). For an early Jacobean audience, schemes to control royal succession through female heirs carried a particular edge — they recalled the succession crises of Elizabeth's reign.

anchor_text: I love and hate her: for she's fair and royal, / And that she hath all courtly parts more exquisite / Than lady, ladies, woman
summary: Cloten's soliloquy is built around an oxymoron — 'I love and hate her' — then elaborates both halves. His description of Imogen as possessing 'all courtly parts more exquisite / Than lady, ladies, woman' is a compacted triple: she surpasses a single lady, the class of ladies generally, and womankind as a whole. The syntax escalates from individual to category to universal.
detail: The rhetorical pattern of beginning with a paradox ('love and hate') and then resolving each term in turn is common in Elizabethan drama for moments of internal conflict. Cloten's escalating 'lady, ladies, woman' functions as an asyndeton (three nouns with no conjunction) that enacts his struggling to find words adequate to Imogen's superiority. The speech is also an involuntary tribute to the woman he intends to rape and the husband he intends to kill: even his hatred acknowledges her worth, which makes his planned violation all the more ugly.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. R. D. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'parts': personal qualities, accomplishments.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1934

The oxymoron and the escalating 'lady, ladies, woman' triple are accurately identified, but labelling the syntax 'asyndeton' is questionable — the three nouns are separated by the phrase 'from every one / The best she hath' in the full text (TLN 1936-1937), not simply juxtaposed without connective; the figure is more paraphrase than strict asyndeton.

anchor_text: What, are you packing, sirrah? / Come hither: ah, you precious pander
summary: 'Packing' means scheming or plotting — acting in conspiracy with others. Cloten suspects Pisanio of being complicit in Imogen's disappearance. 'Sirrah' is an address to a social inferior, sharper than 'sir' and often contemptuous or threatening. 'Pander' means a go-between or pimp — someone who arranges secret meetings between lovers. Cloten is accusing Pisanio of having facilitated Imogen's flight to Posthumus.
detail: All three words need unpacking for a modern reader. 'Packing' in the sense of conspiring (often 'packing with' someone) appears at Richard III 3.1 and Othello 5.2 ('Oh, I were damn'd beneath all depth in hell / But that I did proceed upon just grounds'). 'Sirrah' was a standard male address to servants or inferiors but became very charged when used by someone hostile: Iago calls Roderigo 'sirrah' when threatening him (Othello 5.1). 'Pander' (from Pandare, the go-between in the Troilus and Cressida story) had already become a general insult for any facilitator of illicit love; Hamlet uses it of the court ('a very, very — pajock') and Shakespeare gave the word its own character in Troilus and Cressida.

anchor_text: Where is thy lady? Or, by Jupiter,-- / I will not ask again
summary: Cloten swears 'by Jupiter,' the king of the Roman gods, to threaten Pisanio. Jupiter was the supreme Roman deity — god of sky, thunder, and oaths — and swearing by his name was the most solemn oath in the Roman world. The oath is particularly apt for a play whose British-Roman war will eventually be resolved by the god Jupiter descending in person in Act 5.
detail: The oath 'by Jupiter' recurs throughout Cymbeline (also at 4.2 and 5.4) and is the play's characteristic divine invocation, consistent with its setting in the Augustan Roman world. In Shakespeare's Roman and pseudo-Roman plays characters swear by Jupiter as the sovereign divine power: compare Julius Caesar 2.1, Troilus and Cressida 4.5. The play literalises the oath: Jupiter does appear (5.4) to descend on his eagle and resolve the action, so every 'by Jupiter' is an inadvertent invocation of the god who is actually shaping events. Cloten's casual oath thus has a dramatic irony the character cannot perceive.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.166-252 (Jove as ruler of gods and judge of men); Virgil, Aeneid 1.254-296 (Jupiter foretells destiny).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1949

The oath 'by Jupiter' as the play's characteristic invocation, with the dramatic irony that Jupiter literally descends in 5.4, is a well-established reading in Cymbeline scholarship and directly supported by the text.

anchor_text: With that suit upon my / back, will I ravish her: first kill him, and in her / eyes
summary: Cloten plans to murder Posthumus in front of Imogen, then rape her while wearing Posthumus's own clothes — which Imogen once said she valued more than Cloten himself. The plan enacts both murder and sexual violence as a revenge for the insult to his pride. 'Ravish' means rape. The scheme underscores why Cloten is more than a comic villain: his cruelty is as systematic as the Queen's.
detail: The passage at TLN 2002-2018 is one of the most disturbing in Cymbeline. Cloten's motive is retaliatory humiliation: because Imogen said his 'noble and natural person together with the adornment of my qualities' mattered less than Posthumus's garment (TLN 2007-2009), he will literally enact her words — wearing those clothes while committing the violence. He also plans a 'speech of insultment' over Posthumus's corpse. This is not irrational but a cold logic of humiliation that echoes real early modern accounts of sexual violence as an act of conquest. The garments he asks Pisanio to fetch become central to Imogen's mistaking the headless body of Cloten for her husband (4.2) — a plot irony that turns Cloten's scheme back on itself.

'Ravish' unambiguously means rape in this context (OED sense 1a is correct), and the annotation's reading of the plan — kill Posthumus in Imogen's sight, then rape her in his clothes — is precisely what the text at TLN 2009-2016 states.

anchor_text: Thou bid'st me to my loss: for true to thee / Were to prove false, which I will never be, / To him that is most true
summary: Pisanio closes the scene with a paradox: being 'true' (loyal) to Cloten would make him 'false' (a traitor) to Posthumus, 'him that is most true.' The wordplay on 'true' / 'false' is deliberate — Pisanio's allegiance to genuine worth is itself the definition of truth. The speech also works as an ironic commentary: he has just agreed to serve Cloten while planning to do no such thing.
detail: The antithesis of 'true' and 'false' as a moral compass runs through the late romances: compare The Winter's Tale 1.2 and Pericles 1.2. 'Thou bid'st me to my loss' means 'You send me on an errand that will cost me' — or more pointedly, 'You commission me toward my own ruin' (since if Pisanio were genuinely loyal to Cloten he would be betraying Posthumus). The closing couplet 'This fool's speed / Be cross'd with slowness; labour be his meed' (TLN 2033-2034) is a prayer that Cloten's pursuit be frustrated — 'meed' means reward or payment. The rhymed couplet closes the scene with Pisanio's integrity clearly intact for the audience.

anchor_text: Foundations fly the wretched; such, I mean, Where they should be relieved
summary: The syntax inverts the expected: 'foundations' (solid shelters, houses, charitable institutions) flee from the very people who need them, rather than offering refuge. Imogen means that when she, as a wandering beggar, most needed to find a house, every one seemed to vanish. The construction 'such, I mean, / Where they should be relieved' glosses 'the wretched' mid-sentence — a relative clause looped back to explain the subject.
detail: The word 'foundations' carried a specific Elizabethan sense: an endowed charitable institution or almshouse set up to relieve the poor. Imogen is bitterly noting that such places, which exist precisely to help the destitute, seem to disappear the moment real need arrives. The rhetorical device is a compressed paradox — the helper flees the helpless. This kind of dense mid-clause self-gloss (the appositive 'such, I mean') is characteristic of Cymbeline's deliberately knotted verse style.

anchor_text: To lapse in fulness Is sorer than to lie for need
summary: 'To lapse' means to slip or fall into error. 'Fulness' means abundance, prosperity. Imogen is saying that it is a graver fault to lie when you have everything you need (as the rich do) than to lie out of desperation and want. 'Sorer' means more painful, more grievous.
detail: The passage is a moral aphorism compressed into two lines: the transgression of the comfortable is worse than the transgression of the starving, because the rich have no excuse. Imogen uses it to meditate on Posthumus's betrayal — 'My dear lord! Thou art one o' the false ones' — placing his deception in the worst moral category: falsehood chosen by someone with no need. 'Sorer' (more painful, more serious) is the comparative of 'sore,' here used adverbially.

anchor_text: 'tis some savage hold
summary: 'Hold' means a stronghold, a fortified place, or a den — here a rough cave-dwelling. 'Savage' means wild and uncultivated, not necessarily violent. Imogen is noting that the cave looks like the den of some creature or wild man, not a civilized dwelling.
detail: The word 'hold' for a den or stronghold is common in Shakespeare; see also 'mountain-hold' (a defended or concealed retreat) in other plays. Imogen's wariness is natural: she is a princess in disguise, alone, near starvation, and does not yet know the cave belongs to three essentially decent men. The phrase frames the dramatic irony of what is about to happen — she is walking into safety while expecting danger.

anchor_text: famine, Ere clean it o'erthrow nature, makes it valiant: Plenty and peace breeds cowards: hardness ever Of hardiness is mother
summary: Imogen strings together three balanced, sententious clauses to steel herself to enter the cave. 'Ere clean it o'erthrow nature' means 'before it utterly destroys the body'; 'hardness ever / Of hardiness is mother' is polyptoton (the same root in two forms): 'hardship is always the mother of courage.' 'Cowards' and 'valiant' are the paired opposites that frame the argument: deprivation breeds bravery; comfort breeds cowardice.

anchor_text: Polydote, have proved best woodman and Are master of the feast: Cadwal and I Will play the cook
summary: 'Polydote' and 'Cadwal' are the false names under which Belarius has raised the kidnapped princes Guiderius and Arviragus in the Welsh wilderness. The audience knows these are Cymbeline's lost sons, but the characters do not. 'Woodman' means a hunter; 'master of the feast' credits Guiderius with bringing home the best kill. The domestic division — hunter, cook, servant — shows the three living a Spartan, self-sufficient life stripped of courtly rank.
detail: The false Welsh names are part of Belarius's scheme: by calling them Polydore and Cadwal he has hidden them from Cymbeline's reach. Their hunting-and-cooking routine is the play's sustained emblem of natural virtue stripped of courtly artifice — the romance convention of noble blood expressing itself even in exile. 'Best woodman' would be a compliment in any Elizabethan household; here it replaces the honors of the court that are Guiderius's birthright.

anchor_text: resty sloth Finds the down pillow hard
summary: 'Resty' (also spelled 'rusty' or 'restic') means restive, sluggish, or lazy — one who has grown stiff from idleness. Belarius is saying that the lazy person finds even a feather pillow uncomfortable, while the genuinely tired man can sleep on flint. The maxim reinforces the scene's Stoic theme: hardship is relative to habit.
detail: The word 'resty' derives from 'restive,' originally an animal that refuses to move, and by extension any creature or person sunk in torpor. The contrast between the 'flint' (bare stone) the weary worker can sleep on and the 'down pillow' (feather-stuffed, the height of luxury) the idle man finds hard was a proverbial commonplace in Elizabethan moral writing. Belarius uses it to frame the cave-life as virtuous sufficiency rather than hardship.

anchor_text: By Jupiter, an angel! or, if not, An earthly paragon! Behold divineness No elder than a boy

The exclamation fuses pagan and Christian registers, both reaching for supernatural terms to describe Imogen's beauty — visible even through her male disguise.

anchor_text: All gold and silver rather turn to dirt! As 'tis no better reckon'd, but of those Who worship dirty gods
summary: Arviragus rejects Imogen's offer of payment with a contemptuous outburst: gold and silver are no better than dirt to those who do not make money their god. 'Dirty gods' is an allusion to the worship of money as an idol — those who prize it above honour worship a base, material deity. The speech marks the princes as uncorrupted by courtly greed despite their royal blood.
detail: The contempt for gold is part of the play's sustained contrast between the corrupted court (where Iachimo wins his way with wealth and deception, and the Queen schemes for power) and the wild Welsh cave, which preserves natural virtue. Arviragus's instinct here is literally princely — his contempt for material reward reflects the innate nobility Belarius has been unable to teach out of them. The phrase also glances at classical and biblical critiques of avarice: Mammon worship, Pluto's gold, the Stoic dismissal of material wealth (see Cicero, De Officiis 1.68).

anchor_text: To Milford-Haven
summary: Milford Haven is a large natural harbour in west Wales toward which Imogen has been walking — lured there by the forged letter saying Posthumus would meet her. In the play it is the convergence point for almost every character and for the Roman invasion force. For Shakespeare's Jacobean audience the name had a dynastic ring: Henry Tudor had landed there in 1485 on his way to the throne, founding the dynasty whose line James I claimed.
detail: The name recurs more often in Cymbeline than in any other Shakespeare play, becoming almost a mantra. Its historical charge is part of the play's design: by routing the story through Milford, Shakespeare anchors the legendary British-Roman plot to the real geography of Welsh Tudor origins. When the play ends with a reconciled Britain and Rome, the audience familiar with Milford's Tudor associations could read the settlement as a providential, Tudor-rooted British destiny — a flattery of James I, who styled himself heir to both the Tudor line and the ancient British kings.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles; Tudor dynastic history
sources.citation: Milford Haven, Pembrokeshire; landing-point of Henry Tudor (future Henry VII), August 1485, before Bosworth. Holinshed, Chronicles (1587).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2100

The Henry Tudor 1485 landing identification is historically accurate and is a mainstream scholarly reading of Cymbeline's repeated Milford Haven emphasis; the Jacobean providential-British-destiny gloss is a defensible and widely accepted contextual interpretation.

anchor_text: Fidele, sir
summary: This is the assumed name Imogen gives herself when disguised as a boy-page. 'Fidele' is Italian and Latin for 'faithful.' The name is pointed: she is loyal to Posthumus even as he has ordered her killed. The irony will deepen when her 'brothers' mourn the page 'Fidele' as dead.
detail: The choice of a name meaning 'faithful' is a constant in Cymbeline's allegorical romance mode: characters' names carry moral weight (Posthumus — born after his father's death; Iachimo — the Italian diminutive of Giacomo/James, with a slight villainous Italian colouring). 'Fidele' also pairs with the name Pisanio gave in his directions: a page-name that could be male. When the princes later sing their elegy over the body they believe to be Fidele's, the name's meaning — the faithful one, now 'dead' — carries the full tragic weight.

sources.name: Latin etymology
sources.citation: Latin fidelis, 'faithful, loyal,' from fides, 'faith, trust.' See Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), note on symbolic naming in Shakespeare's romances.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2102

The etymology (Latin fidelis, 'faithful') is correct, the irony that she is loyal to a man who ordered her killed is precisely what the text stages, and the parallel to other symbolic names in the play (Posthumus, Iachimo) is a mainstream critical observation.

anchor_text: Think us no churls, nor measure our good minds By this rude place we live in
summary: 'Churls' means rude, low-born, boorish people — peasants with bad manners. Belarius asks Imogen not to judge their behaviour by their rough dwelling: the cave is crude but its inhabitants are not. 'Rude place' means rough, uncultivated dwelling. The line is central to the play's argument that true nobility is inward, not architectural.
detail: A 'churl' in Old English and Middle English meant a man of the lowest rank; by Shakespeare's time it had generalized to mean any ill-mannered, mean-spirited person. Belarius's disclaimer is delicate — he knows (though Imogen does not) that he and his foster-sons have actual nobility of blood, despite the cave. His words directly address the romance's central theme: that rank and courtesy are independent of material surroundings, and that the princes' instinctive generosity proves their blood.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2107

'Churl' = rude or low-born person is correct, and Belarius's disclaimer as an expression of the play's central theme — inner nobility independent of material surroundings — is textually grounded and critically mainstream.

anchor_text: Would it had been so, that they Had been my father's sons! then had my prize Been less, and so more equal ballasting To thee, Posthumus
summary: Imogen (aside) wishes these admirable young men had been her brothers — true sons of Cymbeline. Her reasoning: had they been royal, her own value as a princess ('my prize') would have been less (she would not have been a unique dynastic prize), and thus a 'more equal ballasting' to the low-born Posthumus. 'Ballasting' means counterweight — as a ship needs equal weight on both sides to stay level. She is saying the marriage would have been less unequal.
detail: The metaphor of 'ballasting' draws on navigation: a ship without proper ballast tips and founders. Imogen is thinking of the social disparity between herself, a king's only heir, and Posthumus, a worthy but landless commoner — the disparity Cymbeline's court resents. If her 'prize' (her dynastic worth) had been lower (because she had brothers to inherit the throne), the match would have been less imbalanced. The syntax is deliberately compressed: 'then had my prize / Been less' means 'then my value as a dynastic asset would have been smaller.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ballast' v., sense 2b: to counterpoise, to balance with an equivalent weight; figuratively, to counterbalance.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2122
OED records figurative uses of 'ballast' v. meaning to counterbalance or counterweight; the nautical-to-figurative extension claimed is well-supported lexicographically.

The navigation-derived metaphor of 'ballasting' as counterweight is accurate, and the interpretation — her dynastic 'prize' being lower would have made the match with landless Posthumus less socially imbalanced — follows directly from the lines.

anchor_text: laying by That nothing-gift of differing multitudes
summary: 'Nothing-gift of differing multitudes' means the worthless, unreliable praise given by crowds who constantly change their minds ('differing' = shifting, inconsistent). Imogen argues that the princes, measured by their own inner virtue ('which their own conscience seal'd them'), outshine great men of court who depend on the fickle approval of the public.

anchor_text: tenor of the emperor's writ
summary: 'Tenor' here means the exact substance or purport of a document — the precise terms it contains, not merely its general drift. A 'writ' is a formal written command issued under authority; 'the emperor's writ' is the official written order from Augustus to the Senate. The First Senator is reading out its exact contents.
detail: In legal and administrative usage, 'tenor' denoted the verbatim or substantive content of an instrument — what it actually says, word for word. OED records the sense as standard in Tudor legal writing. 'Writ' (from Old English writan, to write) was the common term for a formal official document conveying a royal or imperial command. The phrase signals that what follows is an authoritative reading-aloud of the emperor's orders, establishing the scene's bureaucratic, military-logistics register — the machinery of empire mobilizing against one small island.

sources.name: OED

Standard Tudor legal sense of 'tenor' (substantive content of a document) is exactly right for the context of a writ being read aloud, and 'writ' as a formal written imperial command is unambiguous.

anchor_text: Pannonians and Dalmatians, And that the legions now in Gallia
summary: Pannonia (roughly modern Hungary and Austria) and Dalmatia (the Adriatic coast of the Balkans) were volatile Roman frontier provinces. Under Augustus and his successors, they required heavy troop commitments — most dramatically the great Pannonian revolt of 6-9 AD, which Suetonius calls the most dangerous crisis since the Punic Wars. This explains why Rome must raise a supplementary levy of gentry: the regular legions are tied down elsewhere and cannot be pulled for a British expedition.
detail: Tiberius conducted the Pannonian-Dalmatian campaigns from roughly 6-9 AD; Suetonius (Life of Tiberius 16-20) and Velleius Paterculus both describe the crisis. The detail is historically apt for the play's Augustan-era setting and does real dramatic work: it tells the audience that Britain is not Rome's top priority, that this is a second-front war fought with a levy of gentry rather than crack legions — which partly explains why the outnumbered Britons can hold their own at the battle in Act 5. 'Gallia' (Gaul, modern France) was the theater Caius Lucius already commands, from which his forces will be supplemented by the new levy the tribunes are charged with raising.

sources.name: Suetonius, Tiberius
sources.citation: Suetonius, Life of Tiberius 16-20 (the Pannonian revolt of 6-9 AD, described as the most dangerous war since the Punic Wars)

Julius Caesar, Gallic War 4-5' is imprecise (those books cover British expeditions and Belgic revolts, not Gallia as a province per se) but is a secondary 'cf.' note, not the primary claim.

The identification of Pannonia/Dalmatia as volatile frontier provinces requiring Roman troop commitments is historically sound, and the inference that the depleted-legions detail partly motivates the plausible British resistance in Act 5 is a defensible dramatic reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: He creates Lucius preconsul
summary: A proconsul (spelled 'preconsul' in this text) was a Roman official appointed to govern a province or command an army with the full authority of a consul, the Republic's chief magistrate. By Augustus's time the emperor could 'create' — formally appoint — a proconsul to lead a specific military campaign. Caius Lucius, already commanding forces in Gaul, is here given supreme authority over the British war.

anchor_text: whereunto your levy Must be supplyant
summary: 'Supplyant' is an unusual Shakespearean form meaning 'supplementary' or 'filling the deficit' — the new gentry levy must make up the number needed to bring the weakened Gallic legions up to strength for the British campaign. The word is not 'suppliant' (a petitioner) but a distinct formation from 'supply' meaning to reinforce or complete a deficient force.
detail: The OED records 'supply' as a military verb meaning to reinforce or make up a deficiency in troops; 'supplyant' as an adjectival/substantive form is rare and almost unique to Shakespeare. The sense is that the tribunes' levy of gentry is not the main army but a reinforcing draft to fill out the legions already in Gaul, whose numbers are described as 'full weak' (line 2153) for the British war. The construction makes the tribunes' charge precise: they are not raising a new independent force but supplying a gap in an existing one.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'supply' v., sense 5: 'to fill up (a deficiency); to reinforce (a military force)'; cf. 'supplyant' as a derived form

sources.name: Schmidt

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2163

'supplyant' is accurate, but the OED citation cites 'supply' v. sense 5 as the source for the adjectival form 'supplyant', whereas the OED actually holds a separate entry (suppliant adj.² or adj.³) for this 'supplementary' sense with Shakespeare as its only authority — a citation imprecision rather than a fabrication.

The gloss correctly distinguishes 'supplyant' (supplementary reinforcement) from 'suppliant' (petitioner) and the military sense fits the context precisely — the levy fills a gap in existing legions already stationed in Gaul.

anchor_text: a woman's fitness comes by fits
summary: Cloten's 'saving reverence of the word' signals he is about to say something improper. 'Fitness' meant suitability or readiness; 'fits' meant both 'episodes of passion' and 'convulsions' (sudden attacks). In context Cloten makes the words salacious, implying a woman's sexual compliance comes in uncontrollable bursts of feeling that a man must be ready to press. The phrase explains Cloten's next boast that he must 'play the workman' — i.e., act on the opportune moment.
detail: The hedge 'saving reverence of the word' (literally 'asking pardon for the expression') was a standard formula for introducing an unseemly term; Cloten uses it to flag that he is bending 'fitness' to a salacious sense. OED records 'fit' in the sense of a paroxysm or sudden seizure (fit, n.1, sense 3) from the sixteenth century. The bawdy meaning of 'fitness' here is a contextual inference, not a separately attested dictionary sense: the dark context — Cloten is planning rape as well as murder — and the following 'play the workman' make the innuendo unmistakable, encoding his view of Imogen as a passive object to be seized in a moment of vulnerability.

anchor_text: vain-glory for a man and his glass to confer
summary: 'Glass' here means mirror, not a drinking vessel. 'Confer' means to consult or hold conversation with. Cloten argues it is no boastfulness ('vain-glory') for a man to admire himself in his own mirror in the privacy of his own room — a self-serving justification for his vanity.
detail: Both senses were current in Shakespeare's English. 'Glass' for mirror appears throughout the canon (e.g. Richard II uses a mirror as a theatrical prop in 4.1; Hamlet tells the players that drama holds 'a glass up to nature'). 'Confer' as intransitive 'to converse' (rather than the modern transitive 'to confer something') is the normal Elizabethan usage; Onions cites 'confer with' and the bare infinitive as standard. The parenthetical aside — private self-inspection in one's own chamber — mimics legal reasoning, as though Cloten is constructing an argument to excuse himself from the charge of pride.

sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'glass' (mirror) and 'confer' (to converse, consult).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2175

Onions s.v. 'glass' (mirror) is a genuine entry on Perseus/standard editions, and 'confer' as intransitive 'to converse/consult' is well-documented Elizabethan usage supported by Onions; both claims are accurate.

Both 'glass' as mirror and intransitive 'confer' as converse are standard Elizabethan usages, and the reading of Cloten's aside as quasi-legal self-excuse is a mainstream, defensible characterisation of his vanity.

anchor_text: yet this imperceiverant thing loves him in my despite
summary: 'Imperceiverant' means unable to perceive or understand — perceptually deficient. Cloten calls Imogen an 'imperceiverant thing' because she fails to see what he takes to be his obvious superiority to Posthumus in youth, strength, wealth, birth, military service, and single combat. The word appears nowhere else in Shakespeare and may be his own coinage. 'In my despite' means in defiance of me, or to spite me.
detail: The word is a hapax (recorded only here) and is almost certainly Shakespeare's formation from 'perceive' on the Latin privative prefix. The coinage suits the play's ornate, knotted diction in the romances. 'Despite' (noun) = contempt, defiance — 'in my despite' is a compressed phrase meaning 'to my contempt' or 'in defiance of my merits.' The whole catalogue that precedes — lines, youth, strength, fortune, time's advantage, birth, general service, single combat — is a point-by-point blazon of masculine worth grotesquely misapplied to a man Imogen has rejected and who plans to murder her husband. The coinage 'imperceiverant' neatly collapses Cloten's frustration into a single insulting pseudo-technical term.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'imperceiverant' (only citation: Cymbeline 4.1); s.v. 'despite' n. (contempt, defiance, sense 1b).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2181

OED does record 'imperceiverant' with the single Cymbeline citation (the Folio 'imperseuerant' is a recognized emendation), and OED s.v. 'despite' n. (contempt, defiance) is a genuine, well-attested sense; both source claims hold.

The hapax status is accurate, the Latin privative-prefix derivation is the only plausible etymology, and 'in my despite' as 'in defiance of/to my contempt' is standard Elizabethan idiom — no over-reach.

anchor_text: What mortality is!
summary: 'Mortality' here does not mean death but humankind — the condition of being mortal, i.e. mere human beings. Cloten is exclaiming at the incomprehensibility of people: 'What a thing humanity is!' (that a woman would love an inferior man). A student reading this as a comment on death will misread the sentence entirely.
detail: The sense 'the condition of being mortal; human beings as a class' is well established in Elizabethan English and appears at several points in Shakespeare (e.g. Timon of Athens 5.1, 'our mortalitie'; Measure for Measure 3.1, 'this sensible warm motion to become / A kneaded clod'). The exclamatory structure 'What X is!' (= 'How extraordinary X is!') is a standard rhetorical figure; Onions notes 'mortality' used in the sense of mankind. The word is placed as a kind of summary shrug after Cloten's self-pitying catalogue — the gap between his stated superiority and Imogen's indifference is attributed to the general irrationality of the human race.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'mortality' (sense 2: human nature, the condition of man; mankind).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2182

Onions s.v. 'mortality' records a sense of 'human nature / the condition of man' consistent with the annotation's claim, and the exclamatory usage meaning 'mankind' is standard in Shakespeare scholarship.

The sense 'mortality' = humankind / the condition of being mortal is well established in the period and is the only reading that makes grammatical sense as Cloten's summarising exclamation; the warning against misreading it as a comment on death is sound and pedagogically useful.

anchor_text: clay and clay differs in dignity, Whose dust is both alike
summary: Imogen (disguised as Fidele) uses a paradox: clay is clay — all humans are made of the same dust — yet society ranks them in 'dignity' (rank, worth). The line signals her awareness that, despite Arviragus's fraternal warmth, she is ostensibly a servant-page, not his social equal. The paradox draws on the biblical dust-to-dust idea as well as the Stoic levelling of death.
detail: The figure anticipates the dirge later in the scene ('golden lads and girls all must, / As chimney-sweepers, come to dust'). Imogen's phrasing acknowledges hierarchical difference while quietly insisting on a deeper equality — the very tension that runs through her disguise: she is more 'royal' than the cave-bred strangers she serves, yet they are in truth her brothers and their buried royal nature equals hers. The compressed syntax ('clay and clay differs... Whose dust') is typical of Cymbeline's knotted late style.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'dignity' (worth, rank, degree of excellence).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2199

The paradox of equal dust despite unequal dignity is sound, the connection to the dirge's 'come to dust' is standard critical reading, and the Stoic levelling at death is well-attested; nothing here overreaches.

anchor_text: not so citizen a wanton as To seem to die ere sick
summary: 'Citizen' here is used as an adjective meaning 'townbred, soft, or pampered' — the kind of person who makes a great show of illness. A 'wanton' is a wilful, self-indulgent person. Imogen says she is not so weak and town-bred as to perform illness ('seem to die') before she is actually sick.

'Citizen' as adj. meaning soft or town-bred is a defensible and well-glossed Elizabethan usage, and 'wanton' as self-indulgent person fits the line straightforwardly.

anchor_text: Stick to your journal course: the breach of custom Is breach of all
summary: 'Journal' means daily, regular — from Latin diurnalis via French. Imogen urges Belarius and the brothers to keep to their everyday routine ('daily course') of hunting. 'The breach of custom is breach of all' is a compressed maxim: breaking an established habit throws everything into disorder.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2205
Onions s.v. 'journal' (daily, quotidian) is real and the Pericles 4.4 cross-reference ('the journal tide') is correct.
'Journal' meaning daily is standard, and the compressed maxim about custom is a fair reading of Imogen's insistence that the men keep to their routine.

anchor_text: O noble strain! O worthiness of nature! breed of greatness!
summary: Belarius's aside uses the language of blood and breeding: 'strain' means lineage or hereditary disposition, 'breed' means the stock one comes from. He marvels that the boys' instinctive nobility ('worthiness of nature') reveals their royal birth even though they have never known it. The passage voices the play's central theme: that royal blood announces itself even in total ignorance of courtly education.
detail: The idea that innate nobility — 'invisible instinct' as Belarius calls it later — cannot be suppressed by environment was contested in Elizabethan debate about nature versus nurture. Belarius also knows who they really are, so his wonder is partly ironic; the speech dramatizes a providential design in which birth asserts itself without being taught. 'Nature hath meal and bran, contempt and grace' uses a milling metaphor: nature produces both fine flour (grace) and rough bran (contempt), and the boys are the fine grain despite their rustic life.
