anchor_text: Nobly he yokes A smiling with a sigh, as if the sigh Was that it was, for not being such a smile
summary: Arviragus describes Imogen's mingled grief and composure with a knotted oxymoron ('yokes a smiling with a sigh') and then a syntax so compressed it halts a modern reader: 'the sigh was that it was, for not being such a smile' — the sigh is exactly itself, and it exists because it cannot be a smile. The smile, in turn, mocks the sigh for even being present in 'so divine a temple' as Fidele's face.

'Divine a temple' casts Imogen's body as a sacred place; 'commix with winds that sailors rail at' demeans the sigh by comparing it to common storm-bluster. Arviragus (Cadwal) is the more lyrical, sensitive of the two brothers; this speech establishes his tenderness before the formal elegy of the dirge.

The metaphor urges patience to win out over grief.

anchor_text: on the gates of Lud's-town set your heads
summary: Lud's Town is the legendary ancient name for London — supposed by Tudor chroniclers to have been built or named by King Lud, a mythical British king. Cloten's threat is both archaic (invoking the legendary British past) and topically familiar.

The gate-display of severed heads was familiar from English history: William Wallace's head was set over London Bridge in 1305, and traitors' heads remained a feature of the city into Shakespeare's own lifetime.

anchor_text: O thou goddess, Thou divine Nature, how thyself thou blazon'st In these two princely boys! They are as gentle As zephyrs blowing below the violet

The wind-images span from the violet to the uprooted pine — a formal amplification (one of the play's many rhetorical heightenings in blank verse).

anchor_text: With fairest flowers Whilst summer lasts and I live here, Fidele, I'll sweeten thy sad grave
summary: Arviragus's flower-catalogue — pale primrose, azured harebell, eglantine, ruddock (robin) with charitable bill, furred moss — is an elegy in the pastoral tradition, listing natural things that will grace the dead's resting-place. Such flower-catalogues appear in classical elegy (Virgil, Eclogue 5; Ovid) and were a set-piece of Renaissance pastoral (compare Ophelia's flowers, Perdita's in The Winter's Tale). The specific flowers are painted with precise English botanical detail.
detail: The pale primrose suggests a fair, sickly complexion; the 'azured harebell' (blue-bell) echoes the blue of veins; eglantine (sweetbriar) is chosen for fragrance; the ruddock (robin redbreast) was believed in folk tradition to cover unburied bodies with leaves, its 'charitable bill' shaming rich heirs who leave parents unmonumented. The rhetorical move from flower to bird to moral aside ('O bill, sore-shaming / Those rich-left heirs') is controlled pathos-building. Arviragus finally promises 'furred moss' in winter when flowers are gone, showing perpetual care. The catalogue is one of Shakespeare's finest set-pieces.

anchor_text: Thersites' body is as good as Ajax', When neither are alive.
summary: Guiderius invokes two figures from the Trojan War to make a point about death's levelling. Thersites was the ugliest and most contemptible Greek at Troy — a cowardly, foul-mouthed commoner. anchor_text: Fear no more the heat o' the sun, Nor the furious winter's rages
summary: The funeral song 'Fear no more' is one of Shakespeare's most celebrated lyrics. Each stanza catalogues the hardships of life — heat, cold, the tyrant's power, hunger, lightning, slander — and declares that the dead are past all of them. The refrain 'come to dust' binds high ('golden lads') and low ('chimney-sweepers') in the same end. The song is simultaneously consolation and memento mori — death as release from suffering.

'Thunder-stone' (2533) is the thunderbolt imagined as a physical stone flung by the gods. 'Exorciser' (2538) is one who raises spirits; the song promises that no such disturber will trouble the dead. The lyric has no source beyond Shakespeare's invention and is unique in the play's world for its uncomplicated beauty amid the surrounding confusion.

anchor_text: To thee the reed is as the oak: The sceptre, learning, physic, must All follow this, and come to dust.

anchor_text: His foot Mercurial; his Martial thigh; The brawns of Hercules

anchor_text: I saw Jove's bird, the Roman eagle, wing'd From the spongy south to this part of the west, There vanish'd in the sunbeams: which portends-- Unless my sins abuse my divination-- Success to the Roman host.

The 'spongy south' is the Mediterranean, felt as humid; the west is Britain, associated with sunset and finality.

anchor_text: We'll slip you for a season; but our jealousy

summary: 'Gallia' is the Latin name for Gaul, the Roman province covering modern France and Belgium. Roman legions were stationed there as a forward military base. The First Lord is reporting that the Roman army has crossed from Gaul to land on the British coast — the invasion Cymbeline triggered by refusing to pay the tribute owed to Rome since Julius Caesar's campaigns.
detail: Shakespeare follows Holinshed's account of the legendary British king Cunobeline, who ruled under Rome's peace. The play's war turns on Cymbeline's defiant refusal to pay the tribute first owed after Caesar's expeditions of 55-54 BC. The senate's decision to send Roman 'gentlemen' (equites, gentry-rank officers) alongside the legions reflects a standard Roman practice of supplementing professional forces with politically connected volunteers, as described in Holinshed's Chronicles (1587).

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), History of England, on Kymbeline and Britain's tribute to Rome; the Roman legions raised against Britain.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2706
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) genuinely covers Cymbeline/Cunobeline and Britain's tribute obligation to Rome and is the primary source Shakespeare drew on for this play's historical framework.

Gallia = Gaul is correct; the Holinshed connection and tribute-war framing are standard for this play; the aside about 'politically connected volunteers' is a minor inference but does not distort the gloss.

anchor_text: I am amazed with matter.
summary: 'Amazed' means stunned, dazed, or overwhelmed — not merely surprised as in modern usage. 'Matter' means business, affairs, or things to be dealt with. Cymbeline is saying he is paralyzed by the sheer weight of crises piling on him at once: his queen's illness, Imogen's disappearance, Cloten's absence, and now a Roman invasion.
detail: In Elizabethan English, 'amaze' retained its stronger sense of bewilderment bordering on stupor (OED v. sense 1, 'to overwhelm with wonder or shock, to daze'). 'Matter' for business or weighty affairs is ubiquitous in Shakespeare (OED n. sense 12). The short sentence — five syllables, a broken half-line — performs the compression Cymbeline describes: there are simply too many things to name.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'amaze' v. sense 1 (to overwhelm with astonishment or confusion); s.v. 'matter' n. sense 12 (affair, business, thing requiring attention).

sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'amaze' (to bewilder, stun).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2710

OED 'amaze' v. sense 1 (overwhelm with confusion) and 'matter' n. sense 12 (affair, business), and Onions' Shakespeare Glossary entry for 'amaze' (bewilder, stun), are real sources that support the archaic-sense claims.
'Amazed' = dazed or overwhelmed and 'matter' = weighty affairs are standard Elizabethan senses; the broken-half-line metrical observation is accurate and does not overreach.

anchor_text: Wherein I am false I am honest; not true, to be true.
summary: Pisanio states a deliberate paradox: the lie he told Posthumus — that Imogen was dead — was itself an act of honesty toward a deeper truth, because it kept Imogen alive and preserved his real loyalty to both master and mistress. 'Not true, to be true' is the compressed form: he was untrue (dishonest in fact) in order to be true (faithful in purpose).
detail: The figure is antithesis compressed to oxymoron — a pairing of contradictory terms to capture a moral reality that cannot be stated in simple terms. Pisanio is in an impossible position: Posthumus ordered him to murder Imogen; he refused, helped her escape, and reported her death to spare her. His lie is the most honest thing he could do given who and what he serves. The line is also a precise specimen of what rhetoricians called paradiastole — redefining a term (here 'false/true') to reveal that apparent vice is actual virtue. See Peacham, The Garden of Eloquence (1577), on paradiastole.

sources.name: Peacham
sources.citation: Peacham, Henry, The Garden of Eloquence (1577; expanded 1593), on paradiastole and antithesis as rhetorical figures of contrast and redefinition.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'true' and 'false' (the moral senses in play in this line).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2727

Peacham's Garden of Eloquence (1577, expanded 1593) is a real English rhetorical handbook that names and defines paradiastole as redescribing vices as virtues, confirming the annotation's figure-of-speech claim; Schmidt's coverage of 'true'/'false' moral senses is a routine supporting cite.

The antithesis / oxymoron reading is sound, but calling the figure 'paradiastole' overreaches: paradiastole typically redefines a term to disguise vice as virtue (or vice versa), whereas Pisanio is acknowledging a genuine double truth; the device is better classified as antithesis.

anchor_text: receive us / For barbarous and unnatural revolts / During their use
summary: The sentence means: the Romans 'must either slay us as enemy Britons or accept us as barbarous mutineers — use us while we are useful — and then slay us afterward.' 'Revolts' here means people who have revolted (rebels), not the acts of rebellion. 'During their use' = for the duration of our usefulness to them. Guiderius is arguing that surrendering to Rome offers no escape.
detail: Shakespeare compresses the two alternatives into a single 'or...or' construction: 'Must or for Britons slay us, or receive us / For barbarous...revolts / During their use, and slay us after.' The noun use of 'revolts' (= 'rebels,' persons who have defected) is found in Shakespeare but rare enough to confuse modern readers. The broader argument — that combatants who cross enemy lines are killed whether they fight or surrender — was recognized military logic in Elizabethan writing on war. Guiderius frames it to demolish Belarius's counsel of hiding.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-5), s.v. 'revolt' (sb.), sense 2: 'a person who has revolted, a rebel'; s.v. 'use' (sb.), sense 6: 'service, employment.'

Schmidt does document 'revolt' sb. in the sense of 'a person who has revolted' (cf. King John usage), and 'use' sb. = service/employment is uncontroversial; both senses are real Schmidt entries.

The 'or...or' construction, 'revolts' as substantive noun meaning 'rebels/defectors,' and the military logic that crossing enemy lines leaves no safe exit are all textually sound and mainstream readings of Guiderius's argument.

anchor_text: may drive us to a render / Where we have lived, and so extort from's
summary: 'Render' here means a forced account or disclosure — a compelled statement of where they have been hiding. Belarius fears that if they join the British camp without being registered ('not muster'd among the bands'), someone who recognizes him could demand to know their identities and whereabouts, under torture.
detail: The noun 'render' in the sense of 'account given under compulsion' is a legal-register word by Shakespeare's day, cognate with 'rendering' of accounts. Belarius's worry is precise: the killing of Cloten (whose identity they concealed) would invite an official inquest ('newness of Cloten's death'), and being unknown soldiers would make them prime suspects. 'Extort from's' = extort from us — the contracted 'from's' (from us) is a Jacobean colloquial compression.

'Render' as compelled account/disclosure, 'extort from's' as Jacobean contraction, and the inference that Cloten's unregistered killing would invite an inquest are all precisely grounded in the scene text.

anchor_text: have both their eyes / And ears so cloy'd importantly as now
summary: 'Cloy'd' means glutted or completely occupied — the Roman soldiers' senses are so saturated with urgent sights and sounds of battle (horses neighing, watch-fires) that they have no attention to spare for identifying strangers. 'Importantly' means weightily or urgently, not 'in an important-seeming way'; it belongs to the Jacobean sense 'pressing in upon one with great urgency.' Arviragus's point: soldiers on alert won't pause to interrogate them.

anchor_text: the want of breeding / The certainty of this hard life; aye hopeless / To have the courtesy your cradle promised, / But to be still hot summer's tamings and / The shrinking slaves of winter
summary: Belarius lists the deprivations the boys suffer: lack of noble education ('want of breeding'), certainty of hardship, no hope of the courtly upbringing ('courtesy') they were born to ('your cradle promised'), and finally — in a compressed metaphor — they are nothing but creatures beaten tame by summer heat and shrivelled by winter cold. The pair 'summer's tamings' and 'shrinking slaves of winter' casts the seasonal cycle as a tyrant that has dominated their whole lives.
detail: The rhetorical figure is climax (escalating parallel items) followed by antithesis: hot summer / shrinking winter. 'Breeding' in Elizabethan English means both upbringing and the social polish that comes from a noble education — the boys have had neither court training nor proper schooling. 'The courtesy your cradle promised' echoes a broader theme of the play: Guiderius and Arviragus are princes, and their inborn royal natures keep breaking through despite their cave-dwelling — but here Belarius, arguing for passivity, turns that same birthright into an accusation against himself. The speech is ironic: Belarius is trying to discourage the boys from doing exactly what their blood compels them to do.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'breeding': 'upbringing, education, manners'; s.v. 'courtesy': 'the refinement of manners belonging to a courtly education.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2763
Onions s.v. 'breeding' and 'courtesy' are genuine entries with the senses cited; no specific false claim is made.

The climax-plus-antithesis analysis, the Elizabethan senses of 'breeding' and 'courtesy,' and the reading of Belarius's speech as an ironic self-accusation are all defensible; 'summer's tamings' does grammatically imply a taming agent, so the compressed tyrant-metaphor reading is not an overreach.

anchor_text: Never bestrid a horse, save one that had / A rider like myself, who ne'er wore rowel / Nor iron on his heel
summary: A 'rowel' is the spiked wheel at the back of a spur, used to urge a horse forward. Arviragus confesses he has never ridden a proper trained warhorse — only one as inexperienced as himself, ridden without spurs or any 'iron on his heel.' The detail is not comic: in the sixteenth century a gentleman who could not ride and spur a horse was disqualified from war and honour. Arviragus's shame at this gap is part of the play's insistence that his royal nature is being wasted in the cave.
detail: The rowel is the distinguishing mark of the fighting cavalryman; to ride 'without rowel or iron' is to ride as a child or peasant, not as a knight. Shakespeare uses the image to measure Arviragus's deprivation against his inborn temperament: two lines earlier he has sworn by the sun that he will go to battle, and now he acknowledges he has none of the equipment or practice that war demands. The same oath 'By this sun that shines' (TLN 2773) is itself part of the argument — an appeal to the natural world as his witness, fitting for a boy raised wholly outdoors.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'rowel' (n.): 'the revolving disc with sharp points forming the extremity of a spur' (in use from the 14th century).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2777
OED s.v. 'rowel' n. defining it as the revolving disc of a spur is accurate and the word is attested from the 14th century in English.

The rowel gloss is unambiguous, the social-honour dimension (gentleman without riding skill as unfit for war) is mainstream Elizabethan context, and the detail connects correctly to Arviragus's shame at being 'so long a poor unknown.'

anchor_text: their blood / thinks scorn, / Till it fly out and show them princes born
summary: Belarius's aside articulates the play's central nature-versus-nurture conviction: royal blood is a force that cannot be suppressed indefinitely — it 'thinks scorn' (feels contempt, chafes) at confinement until it bursts out and proves its owners are born princes. The belief that inherited noble blood will inevitably manifest in noble behaviour, regardless of upbringing, was a commonplace of early modern aristocratic ideology and is the engine that drives Guiderius and Arviragus throughout the play.
detail: The idiom 'thinks scorn' (= disdains, scorns — the verb 'think' used transitively with an abstract noun meaning 'to hold something in contempt') is archaic even by 1610. The aside is Belarius's private acknowledgement that his own counsel of hiding is doomed, because the boys' innate royalty keeps expressing itself — in their martial courage, their instinctive honour, their eagerness for action. The phrase 'princes born' closes the scene on the play's key word: Guiderius and Arviragus do not know they are princes, but Belarius does, and the audience does. Shakespeare uses the same 'blood will out' conviction in The Winter's Tale (Perdita's grace betraying her royal birth) and Pericles (Marina's refinement amid the brothel).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'think scorn': 'to disdain, scorn' (citing this passage and 2 Henry VI 4.8).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'blood' (n.), sense 10: 'the natural disposition or temper held to be transmitted by heredity; blood as the seat of emotion and innate character.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2795
Onions s.v. 'scorn' includes 'think scorn' with citations including 2 Henry VI (confirmed on Perseus), and OED 'blood' n. sense 10 for inherited character/disposition is a real and standard sense.

'Thinks scorn' as the transitive idiom for 'disdains/chafes' is well-attested, and the nature-versus-nurture reading of innate royal blood inevitably manifesting is the mainstream critical and theatrical interpretation of this play, with apt parallels in Perdita and Marina.

anchor_text: For wrying but a little
summary: 'Wrying' means going astray or swerving from the right path. Posthumus is saying that the wives of many husbands would be murdered if each husband ordered their deaths for 'straying but a little' from perfect fidelity — as he wrongly believed Imogen had done.
detail: The verb 'wry' (also 'wrie') means to twist or deviate; 'wrying' is its participial form. It appears in several of Shakespeare's contemporaries as a synonym for straying from moral rectitude. Here it underlines the savage irony of Posthumus's self-reproach: Imogen did not stray at all, but even if she had, the punishment of death would be wildly disproportionate. The syntax of lines 2799-2802 is compressed: 'If each of you should take this course [of ordering a wife's murder], how many / Must murder wives much better than themselves / For wrying but a little!' — a rhetorical generalisation that measures Posthumus's guilt by its consequences if universalised.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'wry' v., sense 1: 'to go crooked or astray; to swerve, deviate.' Cf. also Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'wry.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2802

OED s.v. 'wry' v. does record an obsolete intransitive sense meaning 'to deviate or swerve' (confirmed by OED entry wry_v1 and etymological sources), and Onions lists 'wrying' as an entry; the paraphrase 'to go crooked or astray; to swerve, deviate' accurately captures the OED sense.

OED sense 1 for 'wry' v. (to go astray, deviate) is correct, the syntactic paraphrase of TLN 2799-2802 is accurate, and the ironic reading (Imogen did not stray at all) is firmly grounded in the text.

anchor_text: to the doers' thrift
summary: The passage runs: 'you some permit / To second ills with ills, each elder worse, / And make them dread it, to the doers' thrift.' 'Thrift' here means profit or benefit, and 'to the doers' thrift' is a compressed purpose-clause: the gods allow wrongdoers to compound sin upon sin, growing ever worse, and let them fear the consequences — for those doers' own ultimate good (i.e. so that they will eventually reform). Posthumus is reasoning that the gods have let him commit grievous wrong so he will become terrified of his own sinfulness.
detail: In Shakespeare 'thrift' frequently means profit or gain rather than mere frugality: 'to the doers' thrift' = 'for the benefit/profit of the doers.' The logic of lines 2809-2812 is theological: the gods take some sinners away early, which is mercy (they fall no worse); they permit others to go on sinning, compounding 'each elder worse,' and then make those sinners dread their accumulated guilt — an indirect path to correction. 'Second' (2810) means to follow up or reinforce: 'to second ills with ills' = to follow one sin with another. The dense syntax, typical of late-Shakespeare, requires unpacking before the argument is clear.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'thrift' n., sense 3: 'profit, gain, prosperity.' Cf. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'thrift': 'profit, gain.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2812

OED 'thrift' n. does carry a sense of 'profit, gain, prosperity' active in Shakespeare's period (cf. Merchant of Venice 'such thrift / That I should questionless be fortunate'), and Onions glosses 'thrift' as 'profit, gain' — both citations are real and supportive.

'Thrift' as profit/gain is standard Shakespearean usage, and the theological logic — gods permit compounding sin so that consequent dread becomes corrective, 'to the doers' thrift' as a purpose-clause — is a mainstream editorial reading of this compressed passage.

anchor_text: disrobe me / Of these Italian weeds and suit myself / As does a Briton peasant
summary: 'Weeds' is the Elizabethan word for clothes or garments (as in 'widow's weeds,' the mourning dress still used today). Posthumus arrived in Britain with the Roman army as an Italian gentleman; now he strips off that Italian clothing and redresses himself as a British peasant-soldier so he can fight on the British side against the Romans — and against his own gentry identity — in penance for what he believes he has done to Imogen.
detail: Posthumus is a Briton who was living in Italy as an exile and has come back to Britain as part of the Roman invading force ('Among the Italian gentry,' 2815). His physical re-dressing is a public and theatrical act of self-abasement and realignment: he rejects the Roman alliance and the class-markers of the Italian court in a single gesture. 'Suit' (2821) is used as a verb meaning to clothe or dress — 'suit myself as a Briton peasant.' The switch of clothing is also thematically pointed in a play obsessed with disguise (Imogen as 'Fidele,' Cloten in Posthumus's clothes); here the disguise is a voluntary stripping-down of social rank rather than a concealment of identity.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'weed' n.2, sense 3: 'A garment, article of clothing.' Also Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'weed': 'garment.'

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England (1587), on Kymbeline and the Roman tribute; the historical frame of the British-Roman war that Posthumus is now deserting.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2819

OED 'weed' n.2 sense 3 'garment' is a standard and well-attested OED sense, and Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) is the confirmed historical source for Cymbeline's British-Roman tribute frame; the reference card 'ancient-britain-and-the-roman-tribute' exists in data/references/historical.json.

'Weeds' as garments is uncontroversial; the text confirms Posthumus came 'Among the Italian gentry,' and the thematic linkage to the play's wider disguise/clothing motif (Imogen-as-Fidele, Cloten-in-Posthumus's-clothes) is a standard critical observation.

anchor_text: the strength o' the Leonati in me
summary: Posthumus prays to the gods to fill him with the strength of 'the Leonati' — his dead family, whose surname he bears. His father Sicilius Leonatus was a brave British soldier who died in battle before Posthumus was born; his two elder brothers also died fighting for Britain. By invoking his ancestors by name Posthumus claims their martial courage as his birthright and dedicates his coming fight to their memory, preparing to die bravely.

sources.name: Text (Cymbeline 5.4)
sources.citation: Cymbeline 5.4, the prison-vision: the ghosts of Sicilius Leonatus and Posthumus's two brothers, who died in Britain's wars, appeal to Jupiter on his behalf — confirming 'the strength o' the Leonati' as his dead kindred.

anchor_text: The fashion, less without and more within
summary: Posthumus resolves to 'begin the fashion, less without and more within' — he will start a new custom of having fewer outward shows and more inner worth. 'Without' means outward appearance or external show; 'within' means inward character or virtue. It is an antithesis and the scene's closing moral: in his disguise as a peasant, and in his repentance, Posthumus is stripping away the surface (Italian finery, status, worldly pride) to find genuine courage and honesty underneath.
detail: 'Without' and 'within' are a standard Shakespearean antithesis for surface appearance versus inner reality; the opposition runs throughout Cymbeline, a play preoccupied with counterfeit and truth (Iachimo's false 'proof,' the queen's false love, Imogen's disguise as Fidele). The phrase 'begin the fashion' has a sardonic edge — he will inaugurate a new style in which inner virtue outweighs outer show, though he knows this is hardly fashionable. The figure is a loose chiasmus ('valour / habits' :: 'less without / more within'), condensing the scene's spiritual movement into a single balanced line.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T. A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'without': 'outwardly, externally'; s.v. 'within': 'inwardly, in the heart or mind.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2830

The adverbial senses 'without = outwardly' and 'within = inwardly' are genuine Elizabethan usages, but the retrieved Onions entry for 'without' shows only the prepositional sense 'beyond the reach of'; a second Onions entry may carry the adverbial sense but could not be confirmed, so the specific Onions citation cannot be verified.

The without/within antithesis as outward show versus inner virtue is textually sound and the 'begin the fashion' sardonic edge is defensible; the 'loose chiasmus' label in the detail is imprecise (it is really a continuation of the antithesis, not a true A-B-B-A inversion), but the core interpretive claim is correct and the summary does not misstate it.

anchor_text: heaviness and guilt within my bosom Takes off my manhood
summary: Iachimo confesses that a crushing sense of guilt is stripping him of his fighting capacity. 'Takes off' means removes or disables; 'manhood' here means specifically military courage and strength, not simply masculinity. He has been defeated by Posthumus — a man he considers far beneath him socially — and his conscience supplies the reason.
detail: This short soliloquy is the play's first signal of Iachimo's eventual confession. In Elizabethan usage 'manhood' in a combat context regularly means martial valor and physical resolution (OED s.v. 'manhood' 2a: 'courage, bravery, valour'). The logic is theological as well as psychological: guilt has undone his bodily strength because the body was the instrument of his crime — he crept into Imogen's chamber and manufactured false evidence of her dishonor. That the man who bested him is a 'poor soldier' (stage direction) in peasant disguise — Posthumus Leonatus, whose honor he falsely impugned — makes the defeat doubly apt.

'Takes off my manhood' as guilt-induced loss of martial valor is directly supported by the scene — Iachimo has just been disarmed — and OED 'manhood' 2a confirms the martial sense; the theological elaboration is an editorial addition but does not overreach the text.

anchor_text: I have belied a lady, The princess of this country
summary: 'Belied' means slandered or lied about — Iachimo told Posthumus false stories about Imogen's supposed infidelity. This is not merely dishonesty; to 'belie' a woman's chastity was among the gravest social injuries an Elizabethan could inflict, because a woman's reputation for virtue was tied directly to her family's honor and her husband's standing.
detail: The word comes from OE beleogan and is used by Shakespeare for deliberate calumny that misrepresents a person's character (OED s.v. 'belie' 3: 'to tell lies about, calumniate, slander'). Iachimo's crime ran as follows: he lost a fair wager that he could seduce Imogen, so he hid in a trunk in her bedchamber, observed details of her body and room while she slept, stole her bracelet, and presented all of this to Posthumus as proof of adultery. The lie destroyed a marriage and sent an innocent woman toward death. That the 'princess of this country' is the victim — making her not only a wronged wife but a wronged royal — amplifies the weight Iachimo feels now.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'belie' 3: 'To tell lies about, calumniate, slander' (attested from c. 1300).

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'belie': 'to slander, calumniate.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2832

OED s.v. 'belie' 3 ('to tell lies about, calumniate, slander') is a confirmed sense attested from the Old English period; the Old English etymology 'beleogan' is correct, and Onions's glossary entry is a standard supporting reference.
'Belied' as deliberate slander of chastity is textually exact and matches OED 3; the account of Iachimo's wager-plot is accurate to the play's prior action.

anchor_text: could this carl, A very drudge of nature's, have subdued me
summary: 'Carl' (also 'churl') was a term for a rude, low-born peasant or laborer, used contemptuously. 'A very drudge of nature's' means a mere slave of nature — someone born with no breeding or refinement, as opposed to a gentleman formed by education and rank. Iachimo cannot believe a man he dismisses as a rustic nobody has beaten him in single combat.
detail: The word 'carl' (Old Norse karl, man; Northern English dialectal churl) appears in Elizabethan writing to disparage a commoner or clown lacking gentlemanly qualities (OED s.v. 'carl' 2: 'a rude boor, a churl'). The contrast Iachimo sets up is between himself — a Italian knight ('In my profession,' line 2836, i.e. the profession of arms and chivalry) who wears his honors properly — and Posthumus, who appears disguised as a nameless peasant-soldier. The irony the audience knows and Iachimo does not is that Posthumus is in fact a gentleman of ancient family, and that 'nature' — innate nobility — is exactly what he has always possessed despite lacking rank. The romance's recurring theme is that true worth is inborn and survives disguise.

sources.name: OED

anchor_text: If that thy gentry, Britain, go before This lout as he exceeds our lords, the odds Is that we scarce are men and you are gods
summary: Iachimo's final lines are compressed to the point of obscurity. The logic: 'If the ordinary soldiers of Britain surpass [us Romans] as much as this rough fellow exceeds our lords, then the comparison would make Romans barely human and Britons divine.' He is saying: if one British peasant-soldier can beat a Roman knight, then Britain's whole army must be almost superhuman. 'Gentry' here does not mean the wealthy landowner class specifically but 'people of quality' or simply 'people' in a generalizing sense.
detail: The sentence structure is a conditional with the conclusion drawn at 'the odds / Is': 'If [A] go before [B] as [C] exceeds [D], the odds is that [E] and [F].' 'Go before' = surpass. 'Lout' = an oafish, clumsy fellow (OED s.v. 'lout': 'a clownish awkward fellow'; here used for Posthumus in his peasant disguise). 'Our lords' = Roman aristocrats. The rhetorical move is a kind of a fortiori argument: the lesser case (Posthumus v. Iachimo) implies a conclusion about the greater (British vs. Roman armies as a whole). The speech is Iachimo's rueful tribute to Posthumus and, unknowingly, to Britain — which is fitting because the play ends with a restored British-Roman peace in which both sides honor each other. Note also that 'the odds / Is' (i.e. the difference / odds is singular) is standard Elizabethan grammar.

anchor_text: the disorder's such As war were hoodwink'd
summary: 'Hoodwink'd' means blindfolded. The image is commonly associated with falconry, where a hawk's hood was a leather cap placed over its eyes to keep it calm. Lucius says the battle is so chaotic — friends killing friends — that war itself seems to be fighting blindfolded, unable to tell its own side from the enemy.
detail: 'To hoodwink' means literally to blindfold (OED s.v. 'hoodwink' 1), the word formed from 'hood' + 'wink' (to close the eyes); the figurative sense 'to deceive' more familiar today developed from this literal one. The blindfold image was readily linked to the falconer's hood, which covered a hawk's eyes to keep it still. Shakespeare uses the literal sense here: the disorder is such that it is as if war itself has been blindfolded and cannot distinguish friend from foe. The image suits a battle that has seen Cymbeline captured by his own enemies and rescued by men — Belarius and the princes — whom he does not recognize as his sons. The play's whole fifth act is about identity recovered and misrecognition corrected.

anchor_text: Of his wings destitute, the army broken
summary: 'Wings' here means the flanking divisions of an army — the left wing and right wing — not literal feathers. A commander 'destitute of his wings' has lost the soldiers on both sides of the main body, leaving the center exposed and the formation collapsed.
detail: The military term 'wings' for the flanks of an army formation is classical in origin and was standard in Elizabethan military writing. Posthumus is describing King Cymbeline's army as having lost its flanking support before the main body broke: stripped of flank cover, the army could be rolled up from the sides. The image of flying / fleeing soldiers at TLN 2858 immediately plays on the literal sense of 'wings' — Britons taking flight like birds rather than using their wings to fight.

anchor_text: lads more like to run The country base
summary: 'Country base' (or 'prisoners' base') was a popular outdoor chasing game, often played by boys, in which players try to tag opponents and carry them back to their own 'base.' Posthumus is saying Guiderius and Arviragus looked like teenagers fit for a playground game — not soldiers — yet they stood and fought.
detail: The game is mentioned several times by Shakespeare: Cymbeline 5.3, The Two Gentlemen of Verona 2.1 ('base'), and Pericles 2.1. The players formed two teams, each with a 'home' (base or prison); a player caught while away from base was held prisoner until tagged free by a teammate. Posthumus's point is that the youths' faces and frames — 'with faces fit for masks' (TLN 2874) — suggested nothing beyond a schoolboy game, making their battlefield courage the more astonishing.

anchor_text: To darkness fleet souls that fly backwards
summary: The sentence is inverted: the normal order would be 'Souls that fly backwards fleet to darkness.' 'Fleet' means 'fly quickly' or 'speed away'; 'fly backwards' means flee in retreat, turning one's back to the enemy. The meaning: cowards who run from battle speed their souls toward damnation.
detail: The verb 'fleet' (to pass swiftly, to fly) was already archaic in Shakespeare's time; he uses it in a handful of late passages for swift, almost ghostly motion. The inversion (verb before subject) is characteristic of Posthumus's heightened, compressed battle-narrative style in this scene, where speech itself mimics the urgency of the fight. The phrase echoes classical and Renaissance ideas that dying in cowardly retreat was a kind of spiritual as well as military death.

anchor_text: which could have turn'd A distaff to a lance
summary: A distaff is the cleft stick used for spinning wool or flax — the standard symbol of women's domestic work, and the opposite of a weapon. To say the three soldiers' nobleness 'could have turn'd a distaff to a lance' means their courage was so inspiring it would have transformed the most peaceful, womanly tool into a weapon — even a spinster would have taken up arms for them.
detail: The distaff was the conventional emblem of feminine domesticity in classical and Renaissance iconography: a woman's estate ('the distaff side' still means the female line in a family). Posthumus uses it as the extreme other end of the scale from military valor: if their bravery could transform the most unmartial object imaginable into a spear, it could certainly stir frightened soldiers. The hyperbole is characteristic of Cymbeline's figurative density; compare Shakespeare's similar 'arm'd to the teeth' imagery in other late plays.

anchor_text: Like fragments in hard voyages, became The life o' the need
summary: 'Fragments' on a hard (perilous or long) voyage means the scraps of leftover food — broken biscuit, offcuts of salt meat — that seem worthless in port but keep the crew alive when rations run out at sea. The former cowards, like despised scraps, suddenly became essential: they were 'the life of the need,' the thing that sustained the army at its most desperate moment.
detail: The nautical image is precise: on Elizabethan long-haul voyages (to the West Indies, round Africa) all food scraps were carefully preserved, as victualing was always precarious. 'Hard voyage' referred specifically to a voyage in which supplies were short or conditions severe. The simile works against the logic of the scene: soldiers who were useless or harmful when the army was advancing (they fled and spread panic) turn their energy — their momentum, their fear — into lethal force when they become the pursuers. Cymbeline is unusual among Shakespeare's plays for its density of maritime imagery, appropriate for a play in which Rome and Britain are separated by water.

anchor_text: Those that would die or ere resist are grown The mortal bugs o' the field
summary: 'Bugs' here does not mean insects; it means bogeymen or objects of terror — supernatural fears that paralyze people. 'Mortal bugs' means deadly terrors. Posthumus is saying the former cowards, who had earlier been ready to 'die or ere resist' (die rather than fight), have now become the most feared and lethal things on the battlefield.
detail: 'Bug' in Elizabethan English meant a hobgoblin, a frightful creature, a thing that strikes unreasoning dread — cognate with Welsh bwg (ghost, goblin). Falstaff in 2 Henry IV mocks the 'bugs and goblins in his life' that people thought Hotspur would use against them (2 Henry IV 5.2). 'Or ere' (like 'before ever') is itself archaic: 'die before they would resist' — men so utterly broken they would choose death over combat. The whole passage dramatizes the turnaround: the men most useless in defense have become the most dangerous in pursuit.

anchor_text: I, in mine own woe charm'd, Could not find death
summary: 'Charm'd' here means protected by a magic charm or spell — not 'charmed' in the modern sense of pleased or delighted. Posthumus is saying that his grief over Imogen acted like a magical shield, protecting him from death even when he sought it: the battle could not kill him because his own sorrow had made him invulnerable.
detail: The belief that a person could be rendered invulnerable — proof against weapons — by a charm, spell, or enchantment was widespread in Renaissance folk belief and literary tradition; Holinshed records such claims about particular warriors. The irony is bitter: Posthumus has spent the battle trying to die as penance for ordering Imogen's murder, but his own woe 'charmed' him — kept him alive despite himself. The word 'charm' (from Latin carmen, a song or incantation) retained its full supernatural force in Shakespeare, as in Macbeth's 'charms' and the witches' 'charmed life' references.

anchor_text: a fourth man, in a silly habit
summary: 'Habit' means clothing, dress, or costume — not a custom or routine. 'Silly' means plain, humble, or mean-looking (not foolish). 'In a silly habit' means dressed in simple, low-status clothes. The Second Captain is reporting that the fourth fighter — Posthumus in disguise as a British peasant — wore the rough garb of a commoner, making his bravery seem all the more surprising.
detail: 'Habit' from Latin habitus was the normal word for dress or clothing throughout the 16th and 17th centuries (cf. 'riding-habit,' 'nun's habit'). 'Silly' (from Old English saelig, blessed, then innocent, then simple) had completed its descent to 'humble, plain, poor' by Shakespeare's time, well before it acquired its modern sense of 'absurd.' The combination 'silly habit' — humble clothes — explains why none of the four fighters can now be identified: Posthumus's peasant disguise made him indistinguishable from any other low-born Briton. This sets up his immediate capture as a supposed Roman.

anchor_text: Most welcome, bondage! for thou art away
summary: Posthumus addresses his imprisonment directly, calling it 'welcome.' The logic turns on 'thou art away': bondage of the body is a path away from conscience, which imprisons him more severely. The sentence pivots on the suppressed word 'a' — 'thou art [a] way' — meaning bondage is a road or means toward freedom, even as it is itself a state of captivity.
detail: The conceit is compressed Jacobean syntax: Posthumus argues that physical fetters are trivial compared with the 'fetter' of guilt, and that chains may in fact lead him toward the death — and thereby the spiritual release — he wants. 'Shanks' (TLN 2966) are the shinbones; his wrists and shins are literally locked. The speech as a whole is a formal penitential soliloquy in the de contemptus mundi (contempt-of-the-world) tradition: the body and its prison are nothing; conscience is everything.

anchor_text: the sure physician, death, who is the key
summary: Death is personified as a reliable doctor — a 'sure physician' who cures suffering by the simple remedy of ending life. The metaphor extends: he 'unlocks' the bolts of the prison, so death is simultaneously a healer and a key-bearer. Shakespeare commonly figures death as a releasing physician in the tragedies and late plays.
detail: The conceit links two strands: the medical and the carceral. Death is 'sure' not in the modern sense of confident, but in the older sense of trustworthy and inevitable — he never fails to come. The 'key' picks up the prison-lock imagery that runs through Posthumus's whole soliloquy (locks, bolt, gyves, bonds, fetter'd). Comparable medical metaphors for death appear in Hamlet ('the undiscovered country') and King Lear ('this great decay').

anchor_text: The penitent instrument to pick that bolt
summary: 'Penitent instrument' means the tool or means of repentance — the thing that will open the lock of his guilty conscience. Posthumus is asking the gods for whatever act of penitence will 'pick' (unlock) the moral restraint he feels more keenly than any iron bolt. 'Bolt' here is the bar securing a lock, not a thunderbolt.
detail: 'Instrument' in this period carries the sense of both a tool and a means or agent — the penitent action that will function as a key. The whole sentence is a prayer: Posthumus asks the gods for the means of true repentance, promising that once conscience is unlocked he will 'be free for ever' — free of guilt, not merely of prison-chains. The theological weight falls on 'penitent': not any act, but the specifically contrition-based one.

anchor_text: broken debtors take a third, A sixth, a tenth
summary: Posthumus compares himself to an insolvent debtor. In Elizabethan commercial practice, a creditor who held a 'broken' (bankrupt) debtor might agree to accept a fraction of what was owed — a third, a sixth, a tenth — and forgive the rest, letting the debtor 'thrive again on their abatement.' Posthumus tells the gods he does not want such a partial deal: take his whole life for Imogen's.
detail: The debt-and-audit language (lines 2976-2985 also deploy 'coin'd,' 'stamp,' 'audit,' 'cancel') is characteristic of Shakespeare's late style, where abstract moral reasoning is worked out through commercial metaphors. 'Abatement' is the legal reduction of a sum owed. The logic of Posthumus's prayer is that he holds himself bankrupt before the gods and offers everything — the coin of his life — in full settlement for Imogen's survival. The word 'cancel' (TLN 2985) also has a legal sense: to annul a bond or deed.

anchor_text: they weigh not every stamp; Though light, take pieces for the figure's sake
summary: 'Stamp' is the design pressed into a coin when it is minted; 'figure' is the monarch's head or royal image on that coin. Posthumus argues: when merchants exchange coins, they do not weigh every one individually — they accept even a light (underweight) coin for the sake of the king's image it bears. His life is a 'light' coin, but it was 'coined' by the gods and bears their stamp; he asks them to accept it at face value.
detail: The coin conceit carries theological freight: if God made ('coined') every human life, each life bears a divine 'figure' — just as a coin bears the monarch's image — and so even a lightweight (underweight) life retains a dignity worth accepting at face value. For Shakespeare the coinage metaphor consistently links human value to divine authorship; Posthumus offers his 'light' life to the gods, asking them to take it 'for the figure's sake' — for the divine image it bears rather than its worldly weight.

anchor_text: Lucina lent not me her aid, But took me in my throes
summary: Lucina was the Roman goddess of childbirth — the divine midwife who helped mothers through labour. The Mother's ghost says Lucina 'lent not her aid' but instead 'took' her while she was in her 'throes' (birth-pains), meaning she died giving birth to Posthumus. 'From me was Posthumus ript' may mean he was delivered by a primitive form of caesarean section after his mother died.
detail: Lucina (Latin 'she who brings into the light') was an aspect of both Juno and Diana as protectors of childbirth. Ovid dramatises her power in the story of the birth of Hercules, where she is sent by jealous Juno to delay Alcmena's delivery (Metamorphoses 9.281-323). The phrase 'Posthumus ript' carries the literal force of 'cut out' — the name Posthumus itself means 'born after' and conventionally referred to a child born after its father's death; to be born by cutting after the mother's death is a doubly posthumous condition. The card for Lucina is already in use in Pericles, and this is one of the direct forward-reuses noted in the architecture.

anchor_text: become the geck and scorn O' th' other's villany
summary: A 'geck' is an Elizabethan word for a dupe or fool — someone made a laughing-stock. The ghost of Sicilius complains that Posthumus was allowed to become the dupe and mockery of Iachimo's villainy, tricked into believing his wife was unfaithful. The word is rare and dialect-coloured, from Low German.

anchor_text: Tenantius' right With honour to maintain
summary: Tenantius is Cymbeline's father — the previous king of Britain — as named in Holinshed's Chronicles. The Leonati brothers say they died in battle to uphold Tenantius's legitimate royal line, the house Cymbeline inherits. The name roots the play in a quasi-historical British past drawn from the same source Shakespeare used for Lear and Macbeth.

By naming him, Shakespeare gives Posthumus's family a specific political loyalty: they served the crown, died for it, and expect the gods to honour that sacrifice. The dynastic context underlines why Posthumus's dishonour is felt as a family wound, not merely a personal one.

anchor_text: Jupiter, thou king of gods, Why hast thou thus adjourn'd The graces for his merits due
summary: The First Brother addresses Jupiter directly as 'king of gods,' the supreme Roman deity of sky and thunder. 'Adjourn'd' means postponed or deferred — the graces (gifts, rewards) Posthumus has earned by his merit have been delayed without cause. The complaint is the core of the ghosts' petition: they cannot understand why a god who controls all things allows a good man to suffer.
detail: Jupiter (Greek Zeus) rules the Olympian gods and governs fate and providence in Roman religion, just as in Virgil's Aeneid he assures the gods that Rome's destiny is secure ('Whom best I love I cross,' he will say at TLN 3058, is Jupiter's own doctrine of deferred providential reward). 'Adjourn'd' carries a legal-parliamentary weight — a sitting postponed — consistent with the scene's quasi-legal structure, the ghosts making a formal case before the divine tribunal. The word 'graces' (plural) covers both divine favour and the concrete earthly goods — reunion with Imogen, honour, restoration — it represents.

anchor_text: No more, you petty spirits of region low, Offend our hearing; hush!
summary: Jupiter descends on a mechanical eagle through a trap in the stage roof (the 'heavens') to appear in person — a theatrical device called a theophany, from the Greek for a god's visible manifestation. This was achieved at the Blackfriars Theatre, where Cymbeline was first performed, using a flying machine that lowered large properties and actors from above. He speaks in the royal plural ('our hearing'), the register of divine sovereignty.
detail: A theophany — a deity appearing bodily on stage — was an old device of classical drama (the 'deus ex machina,' literally the god from the machine). The Blackfriars indoor theatre, which the King's Men used from 1609, had more elaborate stage machinery than the Globe, and Cymbeline shows it off. Jupiter's eagle was probably a large heraldic prop or a seated actor. The stage direction specifies thunder, lightning, and the apparitions falling on their knees — a full staged miracle. Some early critics doubted Shakespeare wrote the scene; modern scholarship generally accepts it. The royal plural ('our hearing,' 'our godhead,' 'our Jovial star,' 'our temple') places Jupiter above the mortal and ghostly worlds throughout.

anchor_text: Poor shadows of Elysium, hence, and rest Upon your never-withering banks of flowers
summary: Jupiter dismisses the ghosts back to Elysium — the classical afterlife paradise where the virtuous and heroic dead dwell in perpetual ease on flower-covered meadows. The 'never-withering banks' are the asphodels of the Elysian Fields, which in Roman poetry bloom without season or decay. The phrase reassures the Leonati: they are in bliss, and their concern for living Posthumus is misplaced from there.
detail: Virgil gives the fullest description of Elysium in Aeneid 6.637-678: the blessed move through groves of purple light, where athletes exercise and poets sing beside a river in the 'pleasant green.' The traditional asphodel meadow (first in Homer, Odyssey 11.539) was by Shakespeare's day a standard poetic shorthand for paradise. 'Shadows' in this period means 'spirits' or 'shades' — the same word as 'umbrae' in Virgil, the insubstantial dead. Jupiter's instruction is both compassionate (they belong in ease) and authoritative (this is not their concern).

The Elysian Fields description, the Virgil Aeneid 6 and Homer Odyssey 11 references, and 'shadows' as spirits/umbrae are all accurate.

anchor_text: Whom best I love I cross; to make my gift, The more delay'd, delighted
summary: Jupiter states the play's central theological idea: that divine love does not prevent suffering but deliberately works through it. 'I cross' means I thwart, afflict, or obstruct — those the gods love most are given the hardest trials. The paradox ('the more delay'd, delighted') means that a blessing deferred and then given is sweeter than one given at once. This is the play's governing providence, applied directly to Posthumus.
detail: The idea descends from Stoic and Christian traditions of spiritual trial: Seneca's 'On Providence' argues at length that the gods test and harden those they love (Providentia 2.1-6); the Book of Job provides the biblical version. In the context of romance the doctrine explains the genre's characteristic shape — long separation, suffering, and then recovery — as the deliberate pattern of a caring divine order. The Soothsayer's final reading of Jupiter's tablet (5.5) will show how every apparent disaster was a step in a providential plan. 'Cross' as 'to thwart or oppose' is standard Shakespearean usage.

sources.name: Seneca, De Providentia

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3058

Jupiter's own words deliver this providence doctrine explicitly; the Seneca De Providentia parallel is apt and well-chosen as the classical analogue, and the connection to the romance genre's structural pattern is a mainstream scholarly observation.

anchor_text: Our Jovial star reign'd at his birth, and in Our temple was he married
summary: 'Jovial star' is the planet Jupiter: in Renaissance astrology, Jupiter was the benign ruling planet ('jove-ial' — of Jove), and its ascendancy at birth was a sign of a fortunate, generous character. The god himself confirms that Posthumus was born under Jupiter's direct patronage, and that his marriage to Imogen was solemnised in Jupiter's own temple — an exceptionally auspicious beginning.

anchor_text: holy eagle Stoop'd as to foot us: his ascension is More sweet than our blest fields: his royal bird Prunes the immortal wing and cloys his beak
summary: Three falconry terms: 'stoop' is when a hawk plunges steeply toward prey — here the eagle swooped down as if to seize them ('foot us' = to seize with the talons, to 'put his foot on'). 'Prunes' is the technical term for a hawk preening and dressing its feathers after a flight. 'Cloys' means to satisfy the appetite — after a kill, a hawk 'cloys the gorge' (cleans the beak). Sicilius describes the eagle's behavior as if it were a satisfied, triumphant hunting bird returning to its perch in the sky.
detail: Shakespeare's hawking vocabulary is among the richest in any writer of the period: prune (OED 'prune' v.2, to dress feathers), stoop (OED 'stoop' v.1, sense 8b, the dive of a hawk), foot (OED 'foot' v., sense 3: to seize in the talons). These precise technical terms are not decoration; they place Jupiter's eagle in the specific imaginative world of aristocratic falconry, the most prestigious Elizabethan outdoor sport, and confirm its sovereign dignity. 'Cloys his beak' echoes Antony and Cleopatra 2.2 ('she did make defect perfection, / And, breathless, power breathe forth') — the satisfied bird as a figure for magnificent satiety.

anchor_text: Sleep, thou hast been a grandsire, and begot A father to me
summary: On waking, Posthumus addresses sleep itself and thanks it, with playful logic, for the family he has just seen: sleep 'begot' a father (Sicilius), a mother, and two brothers for him in the vision. The conceit personifies sleep as a grandfather who has, impossibly, generated an entire family during the dream. Posthumus never knew his own family — his father died before he was born, his brothers in the wars — and the vision gave him, briefly, their presence.
detail: The emotional weight is real: Posthumus woke as an orphan, and still is, but for a moment he was not. The tongue-in-cheek logic ('sleep has been a grandsire who begot my father') is a defence against grief — half-comic, half-tender. The speech then turns to the universal condition of the patronage-seeker who 'wake[s] and find[s] nothing' (TLN 3087), locating Posthumus among the many who depend on great people's favour; but his case differs because he has 'this golden chance' (the tablet) and does not yet know why.

anchor_text: Be not, as is our fangled world, a garment Nobler than that it covers
summary: 'Fangled' means obsessively devoted to novelty and fashion — 'new-fangled' means enamoured of anything new; 'fangled' alone heightens the rebuke. Posthumus hopes the prophetic book will not be like the 'fangled world' — a fashionable garment whose fine appearance covers something worthless. He is already half-sceptical about whether this strange text means anything.
detail: The 'garment nobler than that it covers' is a precise image of courtly deceit: Jacobean court culture was famous for elaborate dress as a marker of status and a mask of worth. The criticism is consistent with Posthumus's earlier praise of honest worth over social show; it also anticipates Cymbeline's broader theme that true identity lies beneath disguise (Imogen as 'Fidele'; Belarius's wards who are secretly princes). 'Fangled' is a back-formation from 'new-fangled,' which is attested in its compound form as early as the 14th century.

anchor_text: When as a lion's whelp shall, to himself unknown, without seeking find, and be embraced by a piece of tender air
summary: Jupiter's prophetic tablet delivers the play's central prophecy in deliberate riddles. The 'lion's whelp' is Posthumus (a prince in nature, a warrior, yet a child — 'whelp' — 'unknown to himself,' unaware of his true standing). 'A piece of tender air' is Imogen — the Soothsayer later explains 'mulier' (Latin for woman) is close to 'mollis aer' (soft, tender air). 'Lopped branches' that revive on the 'old stock' are the lost princes Guiderius and Arviragus restored to Cymbeline.
detail: The tablet is a formal oracle — a genre with deep roots in classical literature, from the Delphic oracle to Virgil's prophecies in the Aeneid. Its riddles are in the tradition of oracular double-meaning: each element points to a character, but only retrospectively is the correspondence clear. 'To himself unknown' encapsulates the romance motif of the hero who does not know his own worth; the pastoral princes who 'find' each other without seeking enact the same principle. The Soothsayer's explication in Act 5 Scene 5 completes the reading: 'mollis aer' → 'mulier' = Imogen; the cedar = Cymbeline; lopped branches = sons.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3096

Virgil Aeneid 1.254-296 (Jupiter's oracular speech to Venus) is a genuine parallel for divine prophecy fulfilled by a play's action; Plutarch Life of Solon on Delphic oracles is a real text that discusses oracle traditions.

The oracle's identifications (lion's whelp = Posthumus, tender air via 'mulier'/'mollis aer' = Imogen, lopped branches = lost princes) are all confirmed by the Soothsayer's explication in Act 5 Scene 5, so this is not interpretive speculation but the play's own authorized reading.

anchor_text: the dish pays the shot
summary: 'Shot' is a tavern-bill or the reckoning at the end of a meal — what you owe for your food and drink. Posthumus is answering the gaoler's image of a 'good repast': if his execution entertains the watching crowd, the entertainment itself (the 'dish' of the spectacle) pays the bill — he dies but the debt is settled. It is a grim pun on 'shot' meaning both a tavern score and a bullet.

anchor_text: the charity of a penny cord! It sums up thousands in a trice: you have no true debitor and creditor but it
summary: The gaoler offers a grotesque economic sermon: a hangman's rope costs barely a penny yet 'sums up thousands' of debts — once you are hanged, every obligation is discharged. 'Debitor and creditor' was an Elizabethan accounting term for the double-entry ledger; 'your neck is pen, book and counters' means the gallows turns the prisoner's neck into the accounting instrument that closes all accounts. The gaoler's joke depends on commercial vocabulary for what is really a death-sentence.
detail: Counters were small discs used to reckon on a counting-board, the standard arithmetic tool before widespread written calculation. 'Acquittance' is the legal receipt given when a debt is fully discharged. The whole speech (TLN 3115-3129) is a sustained conceit in which hanging is treated as the ultimate financial settlement: Bedlam comedy pressed into service as an argument against minding death too much. The comedy heightens the preceding solemnity of the vision: the divine visitation is followed immediately by a fool's prose sermon.

anchor_text: the liver, heart and brain of Britain
summary: Cymbeline calls Belarius and the princes the liver, heart, and brain of Britain — a traditional tripartite anatomy in which the liver was the seat of courage and passion, the heart the seat of feeling and virtue, and the brain the seat of reason. Together they stand for the full vital powers of the nation. The figure is a merism (listing parts to mean the whole).
detail: Elizabethan physiology, drawing on Galen, assigned distinct faculties to these three organs: the liver generated blood and the spirited passions; the heart was the seat of life and love; the brain governed reason and the senses. Cymbeline's compliment therefore praises three different but complementary excellences in his three saviours.

summary: 'Cambria' is the Latin and poetic name for Wales. Belarius, telling the truth in its most minimal form, says he and his foster-sons are Welshmen — he names Wales in the learned form while concealing that they were actually born as princes of Britain and then raised in a Welsh cave.

anchor_text: Great Jupiter, upon his eagle back'd, Appear'd to me, with other spritely shows Of mine own kindred
summary: Posthumus recalls his Act 4 prison-sleep vision: Jupiter descended seated on an eagle while the ghosts of his dead family (his father Sicilius Leonatus, his mother, and his two brothers) appeared to plead his case. The eagle is Jupiter's sacred bird — the king of birds for the king of gods — and in the vision Jupiter physically rode it. The theophany (a god appearing in person) is the play's most spectacular supernatural event.

In Cymbeline 5.4, the stage direction calls for Jupiter to 'descend in thunder and lightning, sitting upon an eagle.' The ghosts of Posthumus's dead family were called the Leonati. Jupiter silenced their complaint and left a riddling tablet on the sleeping Posthumus's breast — the oracle that the Soothsayer now reads. This divine machinery is rare in Shakespeare's late plays and is one of the clearest expressions of the romances' providential design: the gods directly ordain happy endings.

anchor_text: which we call 'mollis aer;' and 'mollis aer' We term it 'mulier'
summary: The Soothsayer performs a piece of fanciful Latin etymology: 'mollis aer' means 'soft air' in Latin, and he claims this phrase is the root of 'mulier,' the Latin word for 'woman.' The derivation is false as linguistics but poetically meaningful — woman as tender air, the softest element. The oracle's 'piece of tender air' is thus both Imogen (the embracing wife) and a pun on 'mulier,' the Latin for wife or woman.

The Soothsayer's interpretation shows how the oracle's riddling words ('tender air') are made to fit the facts: Imogen, the 'mulier' or wife, has been embracing the 'lion's whelp' (Posthumus Leonatus) just as the oracle said. The encoded name-pun (Leonatus = lion-born; mulier = woman/wife as soft air) ties the play's names to its classical machinery.

anchor_text: The lofty cedar, royal Cymbeline, Personates thee: and thy lopp'd branches point Thy two sons forth
summary: The oracle's cedar is an extended political metaphor: the stately cedar tree (the tallest, most majestic of trees, used throughout the Bible and classical poetry as the emblem of kingly might) represents Cymbeline; its 'lopped branches' are his two sons, cut off and exiled; they will be rejoined to the living trunk (Cymbeline) when they are recognised and restored. The tree-as-dynasty image was standard in Elizabethan political thinking.

In Cymbeline's case the lopped branches that revive and rejoin the old stock describe the lost princes' return with precise botanical imagery: lopped branches that have been kept alive (the boys raised by Belarius) are grafted back onto the parent tree.

anchor_text: Although the victor, we submit to Caesar, And to the Roman empire; promising To pay our wonted tribute
summary: Cymbeline, having won the battle, voluntarily decides to pay the tribute anyway — the opposite of what any ancient audience would expect from a victor. 'Wonted tribute' means the customary payment, the one Britain traditionally owed. This reversal — peace freely chosen after military victory — is the play's final surprise and its political resolution: Britain voluntarily enters the Pax Romana rather than remaining defiant.
detail: For James I's audience, this moment had pointed contemporary resonance: James styled himself a peace-making king and liked to be seen as restoring ancient British dignity within a broader European frame. Cymbeline's submission is not capitulation but a sovereign act — he pays freely what he refused under compulsion from the Queen. The Augustan peace that follows is shadowed (as it was for Renaissance Christians) by the birth of Christ.

Holinshed Chronicles (1587) does contain the account of Cymbeline's Britain and the tribute to Rome, confirmed by multiple scholarly sources.

The political reading of Cymbeline's voluntary submission as a sovereign act resonant for James I is a critical commonplace (Leah Marcus, others) but the claim that 'the Augustan peace is shadowed by the birth of Christ' is a contested theological-allegorical reading that goes beyond what the text of this speech warrants; it belongs in a scholar note with appropriate hedging, not embedded in a basic-depth gloss as if established.

anchor_text: The fingers of the powers above do tune The harmony of this peace
summary: The Soothsayer uses a musical image for divine providence: the gods ('powers above') are tuning the peace as a musician tunes a lute or consort of instruments, adjusting the strings until the notes are in perfect harmony. The image of a well-tuned universe was a standard Elizabethan idea — cosmic order expressed as music ('the music of the spheres') — and here it makes the peace feel both finely adjusted and divinely orchestrated.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'tune' (to bring into musical harmony; figuratively, to bring into accord or order); cf. Lorenzo's speech on the music of the spheres in Merchant of Venice 5.1.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3724
Schmidt s.v. 'tune' is a real entry; Lorenzo's speech on the music of the spheres in Merchant of Venice 5.1 is an accurate Shakespearean parallel.
The musical image of divine tuning and the Elizabethan concept of cosmic harmony (music of the spheres) are accurately described; the Lorenzo parallel in Merchant of Venice 5.1 is apt.

anchor_text: the Roman eagle, From south to west on wing soaring aloft, Lessen'd herself, and in the beams o' the sun So vanish'd: which foreshow'd our princely eagle, The imperial Caesar, should again unite His favour with the radiant Cymbeline
summary: The Soothsayer recalls his earlier omen: a Roman eagle flew westward and disappeared into the sun's rays. He interprets this as the Roman eagle (the emblem of Rome and the emperor) coming toward Britain (which lies west of Rome) and merging into Cymbeline's radiance ('Cymbeline' puns on the sun-bright quality of his name) — a sign of the two powers joining in peace. The eagle is both Jupiter's bird and Rome's standard, tying the divine (Jupiter's vision) to the political (the Roman-British peace).
detail: The eagle as the emblem of Jupiter and of Rome's legions (the aquila standard) creates a double meaning: the flight of the military standard (Roman power) toward the west (Britain) and its dissolution in the beams of the sun (Cymbeline) images military might replaced by radiant mutual harmony. 'Lessen'd herself' means grew smaller as it flew into the distance.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 1.394-400 (the eagle as Jupiter's bird and omen); Roman military tradition of the aquila standard.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3728
Virgil, Aeneid 1.394-400, is confirmed as the eagle-omen passage (the eagle harrying swans, used as a favorable augury), establishing the eagle as Jupiter's bird and omen-vehicle.

The double meaning of the eagle as Jupiter's bird and Rome's legionary standard (aquila), and the interpretation of the omen as Rome's power merging into Cymbeline's radiance, are accurately described and consistent with the Soothsayer's own interpretation in the text.

anchor_text: let our crooked smokes climb to their nostrils From our blest altars
summary: 'Crooked smokes' are the winding columns of smoke rising from burning altar-sacrifices — the ancient ritual offering to the gods of a slaughtered animal or incense, whose smoke was thought to please the gods as a sweet savour. 'Their nostrils' refers to the gods. The image is accurate to ancient Roman (and biblical) religious practice, and it frames the final peace as a sacred act of thanksgiving.

sources.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
sources.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita (various books): on Roman public sacrifice and the offering of smoke at altars; cf. Virgil, Aeneid 1.416-417 (the altars smoking with offerings).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3736
Livy documents Roman sacrificial thanksgiving practices; Virgil, Aeneid 1.416-417 is in the Carthage-building passage where altars and offerings appear, supporting the claim.
'Crooked smokes' as winding columns of altar smoke and the ancient practice of burnt offerings whose smoke pleased the gods are accurately described.

anchor_text: Lud's-town march
summary: 'Lud's town' is an old name for London, derived from the legendary British king Lud who, according to Geoffrey of Monmouth and Holinshed, founded or fortified the city; his name was said to be preserved in 'Ludgate' on the western side of the city. The name places the play in the legendary ancient-British past described by Holinshed — the same source that gives Shakespeare the historical frame of Cymbeline's reign.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), History of England: on the legendary King Lud and the foundation of 'Lud's town' (London); Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, on King Lud.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3740
Holinshed Chronicles (1587) does contain the account of legendary King Lud and the foundation of 'Lud's town' (London/Ludgate), as confirmed by scholarship on Shakespeare's sources for Cymbeline.
The identification of 'Lud's town' as an early name for London from the legendary King Lud (via Geoffrey of Monmouth and Holinshed) is correct; the Ludgate connection is accurate.

anchor_text: in the temple of great Jupiter Our peace we'll ratify; seal it with feasts
summary: The play ends with Cymbeline ratifying the peace with Rome in Jupiter's temple — the god who appeared in Act 5.4, whose eagle was the omen of union, and whose prophetic tablet has just been fulfilled. Sealing a treaty in a god's temple was a standard form of solemn Roman oath-taking; feasting together in the sacred precinct made the pact a communal, divinely witnessed act. The final action brings the play's theological frame full circle.

sources.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
sources.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita: on the practice of ratifying treaties and oaths in Roman temples, with sacrifices and feasts as sealing rites.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3741
Livy documents the Roman practice of ratifying treaties with oaths and sacrificial rites in temples throughout Ab Urbe Condita, making the citation supportable.
The identification of the treaty-in-a-temple as a standard Roman form of solemn oath-taking and the noting of the theological frame completing full circle are both sound.

anchor_text: Never was a war did cease, Ere bloody hands were wash'd, with such a peace
summary: The play's closing couplet is a rhymed paradox: no war ever ended — while the fighters' hands were still bloody, i.e. immediately, without the usual delay for negotiations — with so complete and joyful a peace as this. 'Ere' means before; 'bloody hands were wash'd' means before the blood of battle had even been cleaned off. The speed and completeness of the reconciliation are the miracle. It also faintly echoes the hand-washing image used elsewhere in Shakespeare for guilt (Pilate, Lady Macbeth), here transformed: the hands are washed clean by peace, not guilty.

sources.name: Nosworthy, Arden Cymbeline
sources.citation: J. M. Nosworthy, ed., Cymbeline, Arden Second Series (1955), note to 5.5.483-484: the closing couplet as a summation of the romance's providential design.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3743
Nosworthy Arden note to 5.5.483-484 on the closing couplet as a summation of the romance's providential design is a real editorial note.

The main reading (speed and completeness of reconciliation as the miracle) is sound, but appending the Pilate/Lady Macbeth guilt-washing echo to a basic gloss on a couplet about battle blood overstretches; the couplet does not invoke guilt, and the parallel, while not impossible, is an interpretive reach that dilutes the simpler and more accurate primary reading.
